20.13: 20.13 And after God brought me out of my father's house, I said to her, etc. After the word of God was rejected by Judea, all the faithful are brothers and sisters of Christ; hence Matthew 12: Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.
20.14: 20.14 So he took. Allegorically, Abraham signifies Christ, Sarah the Church. Abraham is honored on account of Sarah's beauty, and Christ on account of the Church; hence Psalm 67: God is wonderful in his saints. Sarah had a husband, but he was hidden; the Church has Christ, who is not seen in the world, having been received into heaven.
20.15: 20.15 Wherever it pleases you, etc. Those who had at one time delayed believing through fear of the rulers, at the command of those same rulers betook themselves to the Church, who is the sister and wife of Christ, and spread the glory of Christ and of the Church through all parts of the world.
20.16: 20.16 A thousand pieces of silver, etc. He speaks as if in jest: because she had said that he was her brother who was her husband, and he urges her to remember this in future, lest hereafter, being caught, she incur a similar reproach. A thousand pieces of silver are given to Christ when the eloquent teachers of the world are taken from their pagan way of life to hold and preach the faith of Christ. For a thousand, being the square of ten (the cube), designates the stable and solid doctrine of evangelical preaching.
20.17: 20.17 And Abraham praying. While the Son prays to the Father, the barrenness of the worldly, of the rulers and of the subject peoples is healed.
21.1: 21.1 And the Lord visited Sarah, etc. The figure of circumcision is manifold. For it is, according to the Apostle, a seal of the justice of faith for Abraham and his seed, and a judgment for chastising those who would belong to this seed and faith; and it is a prophecy that the Savior would be born of this seed, who in the present would cleanse us from every sin through baptism, and in the future, after the resurrection, would free us from all corruption of death. The number eight befits the glory of the resurrection: for the Lord rose on the eighth day, that is, after the seventh day, the sabbath; and we too, after the six ages of this world, and the seventh of the sabbath, that is, the rest of souls, which meanwhile is passed in the other life, shall rise as it were at the eighth time, stripped of all the carnal corruptions of concupiscence and the vices in which lust chiefly reigns.
21.4: 21.4 And he circumcised, etc. STRABO. Although circumcision was commanded for many reasons, it especially prefigures Christ, who strips us of the old man through baptism, and in the future, after the resurrection, will circumcise all mortality and corruption. That Isaac was circumcised on the eighth day signifies the eighth age of the world, when the resurrection of the saints will be celebrated universally.
21.8: 21.8 And the child grew, etc. He grows who, arranging ascents in his heart, comes to the solid food of doctrine. Hence: Grow, and you will eat me. The child grew, etc. AUGUSTINE. He made a feast neither on the day of his son's birth nor on the day of his circumcision, but on the day of his weaning: because the joy ought to be great at the spiritual age, when a man has become such as to be fed with solid food, in contrast to those to whom it is said in 1 Cor. 3: I gave you milk to drink, not food.
21.9: 21.9 And when Sarah had seen, etc. JEROME. This is explained in two ways: either that he made sport for idols, according to Exod. 32: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play. Or that against Isaac, as one of greater age, he claimed for himself the rights of the firstborn; and Sarah, hearing this, could not bear it.
21.10: 21.10 Cast out this bondwoman, etc. BEDE, c. 21; ISIDORE, c. 17, on Genesis. It is asked why Sarah earlier wanted to receive a son from the maidservant, or why she now orders him to be driven out with his mother. She does this not inflamed with zeal, but driven by the mystery of prophecy. For Hagar, according to the Apostle, bore a carnal people into slavery; but Sarah bore a spiritual and free one, with that freedom by which Christ has set us free. By this mystery, therefore, it was signified that the former people, begotten in slavery, would not remain forever in the house of Sarah, that is, the Church, nor be heir or partner of the Christians, nor possess the kingdom of glory with the noble son, that is, the faithful people.
21.11: 21.11 He took it hard, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked why Abraham was grieved, since this was a prophecy which he ought to have known better than Sarah: but Sarah said this by a revelation of what had earlier been revealed to him. He, however, was moved by a father's affection, and the Lord afterwards revealed it to him. Or perhaps both at first did not know what it was, and prophecy was uttered through Sarah without her knowing, when she was moved with a woman's mind on account of the maidservant's pride.
21.13: 21.13 Because your seed. AUGUSTINE. It should be noted that Ishmael too is called by God the seed of Abraham, as the Apostle says in Rom. 9: Not the children of the flesh, but the children of the promise are counted as the seed. But this properly belongs to Isaac, who is not a son of the flesh but of the promise, and is spiritual seed by promise, not by flesh.
21.14: 21.14 Taking bread, etc. ALCUIN, FROM BEDE, c. 21. When therefore Abraham cast out Hagar, taking bread, he therefore placed it on her shoulders, etc., down to because some of the people will seek refuge under the shade of the wood of the cross. He took bread and a bottle of water. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis, vol. 3. It is asked how he placed so large a boy on her shoulders. For Ishmael had been circumcised at thirteen years of age before Isaac was born, when Abraham was ninety-nine, and Isaac was born when his father was a hundred; and Ishmael was playing with Isaac when Sarah was moved, certainly with a rather grown boy, who had already been weaned: surely he was more than sixteen years old when he was expelled with his mother. But even if we take it that his playing with the little one was said by recapitulation, before Isaac was weaned, even so a boy of more than thirteen could not be placed on his mother's shoulders; rather it must be understood: he gave her his son, etc. He placed it on her shoulder. JEROME, in the Hebrew Questions. When Isaac was born, Ishmael was thirteen years old, and after Isaac's weaning he is expelled with his mother. Among the Hebrews there is varying opinion, some asserting that the time of his weaning was set in the fifth year, others the twelfth. We, then, to choose the shorter age, reckon that Ishmael was cast out with his mother after eighteen years, and it is not fitting that an adolescent already sat on his mother's neck. But it is true that this is an idiom of the Hebrew language, that every son in comparison with his parents is called an infant and a little child. At Rome too, to this day, all sons are called infants.
21.15: 21.15 She cast the boy, etc. JEROME. What follows: And she cast the boy under one of the fir trees, and going away sat down opposite at a distance, as far as a bow-shot. For she said: I will not see the death of my child, and she sat opposite him; and immediately it is joined: And the boy cried out and wept; and the Lord heard the voice of the boy from heaven, where he was, and the angel said to Hagar: Let no one disturb. For in the Hebrew this is written first: I will not see the death of my boy. So it is read consequently that Hagar sat opposite the boy, and lifted up her voice, and wept, and God heard the voice of the little one. For while the mother wept and awaited her son's death, God heard the boy, whom he had promised would become a great nation. For the mother laments not her own death but her son's. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis, vol. 3. It is asked how the mother, etc., down to as people of any age walking often do.
21.17: 21.17 And God heard. BEDE and ISIDORE, as above. The boy cries out weeping, and God heard; and with the angel pointing, she sees a spring, and this is said on behalf of those who are converted to Christ, and weeping for their sins are heard, and with the eyes of the heart opened see the fountain of water, that is, Christ, who says in John 7: Let him who thirsts come to me and drink. The angel signifies Elijah, through whom the people will come to believe. Hence Malachi 4: Behold I will send you Elijah, who will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children. The angel of the Lord. ISIDORE. Because Scripture names him who speaks to Hagar first an angel, afterwards the Lord, it must be believed that he was the Son of God, who spoke through the law and the prophets, who by obedience to the Father's will is called an angel, but in nature is God.
21.22: 21.22 At the same time. AUGUSTINE, as above. It can be asked when Abraham made a covenant with Abimelech, etc., down to which she did not know.
21.23: 21.23 Swear therefore, etc. Often those who are outside, drawn by the conduct of the faithful, desire to be joined with them and to be better formed by their examples, so as to take counsel both for themselves and for the salvation of their neighbors.
21.31: 21.31 Therefore it was called, etc. There is a twofold reason why it was called Beersheba in the Hebrew: either because Abimelech received seven ewe lambs from the hand of Abraham (for seven is said to be sabee), or because they swore there, for sabaa means an oath. But if we read this reason above this name, it was said by anticipation; as with Bethel and Gilgal, which were called otherwise before they had these names. It should be noted from the earlier passages and the present place that Isaac was not born at the oak of Mamre. Alon in Hebrew is in Latin oak, as it is in the Hebrew, but in Gerar, where Beersheba is a town to this day, which province not long ago, by the division of the governors, was called Palestina Salutaris. Hence Abraham dwelt in the land of the Philistines for many days.
21.33: 21.33 And Abraham, etc. AUGUSTINE. Abraham, as Stephen says, did not receive an inheritance there, not even the space of a foot. But the inheritance is to be understood as that which God was going to give freely, not bought with a price. The space around the well is understood to be that space of purchase for which the seven ewe lambs were given, when Abimelech and Abraham swore to each other.
22.1: 22.1 After these things, etc. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis, vol. 3. James says that God tempts no one; but we commonly say tempt in the sense of prove. James speaks of that temptation by which anyone is entangled in sin. Hence 1 Thess. 1 [3]: Lest perhaps he who tempts have tempted you. For elsewhere it is written in Deut. 13: The Lord your God tempts you, to know whether you love him, that is, to make you know. For a man does not know the strength of his own love unless he learns it by experience.
22.2: 22.2 Take your son, etc. ALCUIN, on Genesis, vol. 1. Abraham was not commanded at once to kill his son, but to lead him for three days to be sacrificed, so that the temptation might be increased by the length of time. For through three days, as his cares grow, the father's heart is tormented, and over that long stretch the father looks upon his son, takes food with him, the boy hangs for so many nights in his father's embrace, lies in his lap, and at every moment the grief of killing his son is heaped up in the father's affection. Whom you love, etc. BEDE on Genesis, c. 22. The temptation is heaped up by the reminder of love and the recalling of his name, and the father's affection is stirred in remembering the promise, because it had been said: In Isaac shall your seed be called, as though, if he were killed, the whole hope of the promise would be frustrated. Go into the land. JEROME, Hebrew Questions, vol. 3. The Hebrews say that this is the mountain on which the temple was afterwards built, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. Hence 2 Chron. 3: They began to build the temple in the second month, on the second day of the month, on Mount Moriah, which is therefore interpreted as illuminating and shining, because there is the debir, that is, the oracle of God, and the spirit that teaches men the truth and inspires prophecies.
22.3: 22.3 Leading his ass, etc. ISIDORE on Genesis, c. 18. The ass signifies the senseless folly of the Jews, which carried all the sacraments and did not know it.
22.4: 22.4 And on the third day. JEROME, as above. It should be noted that from Gerar to Mount Moriah, that is, the seat of the temple, is a journey of three days: and Abraham is said to have reached it on the third day. Wrongly, therefore, do they think that Abraham at that time dwelt at the oak of Mamre, since to Mount Moriah is scarcely a full day's journey. The three days in which they came to the place of sacrifice signify three ages: before the law, from Abraham to Moses; under the law, from Moses to John; thence to the Lord; and whatever remains is the third day of grace, in which third age the sacrifice of Christ was completed.
22.5: 22.5 Wait here, etc. ISIDORE, as above. Hear the Apostle: Blindness in part has happened to Israel, that is, with the ass, until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in, that is, after we have worshiped. When the sacrifice of the cross has been preached through the Gentiles, that is, when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, we shall return to you, that is, and so all Israel shall be saved. The two servants who were sent away and not brought to the place of sacrifice are the Jews, who, living servilely and savoring carnally, did not understand the humility and passion of Christ. Two indeed, because they were to be divided into two parts, which happened when Solomon sinned, when the people was divided in the kingdom, not by an error of impiety, of whom it is said in Jer. 3: rebellious Israel, and faithless Judah. I and the boy, etc. ALCUIN. With unwavering mind he was willing to slay his son. He is to be praised for constancy in offering and for faith in raising him up. For he knew most certainly that God cannot deceive, and that even if the boy were killed, the promise of God would still remain safe. Hence the Apostle in Heb. 11: By faith Abraham did not waver, when he offered his only son, in whom he had received the promise, believing that God is able to raise even from the dead. Abraham said. ISIDORE, as above. Abraham, leading his only son to be sacrificed, signifies God the Father. Abraham received a son in old age, but God does not grow old; yet the promise concerning Christ had in a certain way grown old when he was born. It began from Adam, when it was said: They shall be two in one flesh (Gen. 2); and it was fulfilled in the sixth age of the world. Sarah's old age among the people of God, that is, among the multitude of the prophets, signifies the same thing, because at the end of the times Christ was born from the people of holy souls. Her barrenness signifies that in this world we have been saved in hope, and in Christ, as in Isaac, we have all been born; and this birth the Church brought forth at the end of the times not by nature but by grace. Abraham therefore signifies God the Father, Isaac Christ. For as Abraham offered his only and beloved son as a victim to God, so God the Father handed over his only-begotten Son for us. And as Isaac carried the wood on which he was to be laid, so Christ carried the cross on which he was to be fixed.
22.9: 22.9 And when he had bound, etc. ISIDORE, as above. Isaac, with his feet bound, is placed upon the altar, and Christ is fastened to the cross. But what was prefigured by Isaac was transferred to the ram, because Christ is a sheep. He himself is the son, because he was born; the ram, because he was sacrificed. The ram is caught in the thorns, the cross has horns. For if two pieces of wood are joined together, the shape of a cross is produced. Hence Habakkuk 3: Horns are in his hands. The ram, then, caught by the horns, is Christ crucified. The thorns are briers: the wicked briers which hung up the Lord. For he was hung among the briers of sins. Hence Jeremiah: This people has surrounded me with the thorns of their sins (Jer. 38). Others understand this ram bound in the thorns to be Christ crowned with thorns before the sacrifice.
22.12: 22.12 You have not spared, etc. AUGUSTINE, as above. Did not Abraham spare his son on account of the angel? But in the angel the Lord was prefigured, who is God and the angel of great counsel. For God was in the angel, and spoke in his person. This will appear more in what follows, when it is said: And the angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: By myself I have sworn, says the Lord. For it is not easily found that Christ speaks of the Father as Lord, especially before the incarnation. For according to the flesh this is fittingly said, according to which it is said in Psalm 2: The Lord said to me, etc. But what is said in the same place, c. 9: The Lord said to my Lord, etc., is referred to the prophet who is speaking; as in the saying: The Lord rained from the Lord, that is, our Lord, namely the Son, from our Lord, namely the Father.
22.13: 22.13 A ram. ALCUIN. Historically. The ram which was sacrificed in place of Isaac was not, as we supposed, an apparition, but a real one. Therefore it is thought rather that the angel brought it from elsewhere than that the Lord produced it there from the earth after the work of the six days. A ram among the briers, etc. JEROME in the Hebrew Questions. Aquila put brier or thicket, etc., down to which is said thus in Hebrew.
1.1: 1.1 In the beginning He created, etc. It does not say: In the beginning God said, Let heaven and earth be made. But it said: Let there be light, and there was light, because whatever God made had to be comprehended universally under the name of heaven and earth, and then explained part by part, showing how He made it. Hence it follows: God said, Let it be made, that is, He made it by His Word. Or, because when formless matter, whether spiritual or corporeal, was first being made, it was not to be said: God said, Let it be made; for it was unfitting for God to say 'let it be made,' since imperfection does not imitate the form of the Word, except when the creature has been perfected by the turning of its kind toward the Creator; so that when it is said: God said, Let it be made, we understand that He calls the imperfection of the creature back to Himself. When, therefore, it is said: In the beginning God made heaven and earth, mention is made of the Son, because He is the Beginning; but when it is said: God said, Let it be made, mention is made of Him because He is the Word. By 'beginning' it marks the origin of the creature existing from Him; by 'Word,' the perfection of the creature called back by Him to Himself, so that it is formed by imitating the unchangeable form of the Word. For the Word of God has no formless life, for whom to be is the same as to live, indeed to live is the same as to live blessedly. But the spiritual creature has a formless life, for which to be is not the same as to live, nor to live the same as to live blessedly: because, turned away from the wisdom of God, it lives foolishly and wretchedly. In the beginning, etc. BEDE, Hexameron, bk. 1, vol. 2, col. 13a. Scripture, in introducing the creation of the world, shows in its first word the eternity and omnipotence of God: for the One whom it says created the world in the beginning of times, it signifies to have existed eternally before times. And the One whom it narrates to have created heaven and earth at the beginning of the creation, it declares to be omnipotent by so great a swiftness of working, for whom to will is to do. It is well said, then: In the beginning He created, etc. Both, that is, at once, although both are not spoken at once by man. Hence the prophet shows the earth to have been made in the beginning, saying, Psalm 101: In the beginning, O Lord, You founded the earth, etc. In the beginning, etc. Heaven is not the visible firmament but the empyrean, that is, fiery or intellectual, so called not from heat but from splendor, which was immediately filled with angels. Hence in Job 38: Where were you when the morning stars praised me, etc.? And note that three elements are mentioned here. By the name of heaven we understand air. By the name of earth, the earth itself and the fire that lies hidden in it. The fourth, that is, water, is mentioned in what follows. ALCUIN, on Genesis, vol. 1. In the beginning. In the Son, by whose becoming man it became clear who were heavenly and who earthly. Heaven, the spiritual creature, perfect and blessed from the beginning. Earth, corporeal matter still imperfect. Heaven, the formless matter of spiritual life, as it can exist in itself when not turned to the Creator in whom it is formed. Earth, corporeal matter, without any of the quality that appears in formed matter. BEDE on Genesis, vol. 2, col. 191. Scripture says: You who made the world from formless matter (Wisdom 11). Matter was made from nothing. The appearance of the world was made from formless matter. Accordingly God made two things before all time, the angelic creature and formless matter. For although Solomon says: He who lives forever created all things together (Ecclesiasticus 18), nevertheless in order of origin formless matter precedes the formed species. So God made the world, and the angels, and the soul from nothing; man and the other creatures from something. Ibid., col. 192. There are seven heavens, whose names are these: air, ether, Olympus, space or fiery heaven, firmament, the heaven of the angels, and of the Trinity. Jerome, however, says that the heaven of the Trinity is the first, the second that of the angels, the third the firmament. Mystically. In the beginning God created heaven. That is, those who bore the image of the heavenly. And earth, that is, those who afterward by pride, bearing the image of the earthly man, made themselves deformed. But the earth was empty, because it had put off its good form. And void, of the fruit of good work. And darkness was, namely the privation of the true light; upon the face of the deep, that is, the hearts of the proud.
1.2: 1.2 And the earth was empty, etc. BEDE, Hexameron, vol. 2. He shows what heaven, or of what sort, was made in the beginning with the earth. For he adds this about the earth, which he did not wish to be understood of heaven. For this higher heaven, which is set apart from the turning of the world, as soon as it was created was filled with holy angels: whom the Lord testifies to have been created in the beginning with heaven and earth, saying in Job 38: Where were you when the morning stars praised me, and all the sons of God shouted for joy? He calls the same angels morning stars and sons of God. For concerning the heaven in which the lights are placed, he says later how or when it was made. STRABO. Empty and void. That is, useless, and unfruitful, and unformed. For all the elements were mixed together and confused, and this whole space of air was full of waters; not such as they are now, but they were thin like mists, such as the supercelestial waters still are. BEDE, as above. And darkness was, etc. Those are not to be listened to who reproachfully say that God created darkness before light: for He made no darkness in water or air; but in a distinct order of providence He first created the waters with heaven, and the earth, and when He willed He adorned these with the grace of light. And it must be noted that with heaven two elements of the world were created, in which the other two are inserted, namely water and earth, in which fire and air are present. The waters covered the whole surface of the earth to such a height that they reached up to those places where they now partly remain above the firmament. The earth itself and the water are called formless matter, because all the things that we see either took their beginning from these or from nothing: and before they came into the light, there was nothing from which they could have form. And the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters. AUGUSTINE, bk. 1 on Genesis according to the letter, ch. 5, vol. 3. Whether he called all corporeal matter water, to suggest that from which are made and formed all the things that we see formed on earth in various species out of the moist nature; or the spiritual life before the form of conversion, as if floating. The Spirit of God was borne above, because what He had begun to form and perfect lay subject to the good will of the Creator. It was also said, The Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters, lest God be thought to love by working His works rather from necessity of need than from abundance of beneficence. For it is fittingly suggested first that something begun was there, over which He was borne: not by place, but by a power surpassing all things. And the Spirit of the Lord moved, etc. JEROME on Genesis, vol. 3, col. 939. In the Hebrew it has merahephet, that is, was brooding or was cherishing, in the manner of a bird warming eggs with the heat of a living creature. We understand, therefore, that this is not said of the spirit of the world, as many think, but of the Holy Spirit, who is Himself the giver of life to all things: but if the giver of life, then also the Creator; if the Creator, then also God. Psalm 103: Send forth, he says, Your Spirit and they shall be created. And the Spirit, etc. In whom subsisting we might rest, made alive by His breath and washed by the wave of baptism. And the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters, etc. Just as God, that is the Creator, presided over the floating and confused matter, to distinguish it when He willed. The whole Trinity, therefore, is understood to have worked here: God, that is the Father; the Beginning, the Son; the Spirit of God, the Holy Spirit. And the Spirit, etc. ISIDORE, on Genesis? That is, hearts that were tossed about, which had lost the quiet of the mind, because the Spirit did not rest upon them but was borne above them: as one able to call nature back from confusion to something better. Then throughout the whole text of this Scripture we see six laborious ages, though distinguished as by neighboring boundaries, so that rest may be hoped for in the seventh; and they bear a likeness to the six days in which were made the things that Scripture records God to have made. For the beginning of the human race, in which it began to enjoy this light, is compared to the first day, on which God made light. This age is like the infancy of the whole world, which we think of as one man in proportion to its size. For when a man is first born into the light, he spends the first age, infancy, which extends from Adam to Noah in ten generations: the flood is as it were the evening of this day, because our infancy is blotted out by the flood of forgetfulness.
1.3: 1.3 And God said: Let there be light. AUGUSTINE, On Genesis according to the letter, bk. 1, ch. 17, vol. 3. The light made on the first day is understood as spiritual or corporeal, etc., up to the beginning of the coming morning. BEDE, Hexameron. But if corporeal light was made on the first day, the adornment of the world fittingly begins from light, by which the other things that were to be created could be seen. But if it is asked where it was made, since the deep covered the whole height of the earth? It is clear that it was in those parts which the daily light of the sun now illumines. Nor is it surprising that light can shine in waters, since they are often illumined also by the work of sailors, who, plunged in the deep, send oil from the mouth and light up the waters for themselves: which waters were then far thinner than they are now, in the beginning, because they were not yet gathered into one place. And God said: Let there be light. AUGUSTINE, ibid., ch. 2. Not temporally: for if temporally, then also changeably; if changeably, then also through a subject creature, and light is not the first creature. But perhaps, etc., up to that it may be and that it may remain. Let there be light. AUGUSTINE, ibid., chs. 4, 5, 9. That is, on that condition by which all things subsist timelessly in the wisdom of God, before they exist in themselves. And there was light, that is, the angelic and heavenly substance, in itself temporally; as it was in wisdom, as to its unchangeableness, eternally. Or the formlessness of this creature is noted, namely its imperfection before it was formed in the love of the Creator: for it is formed when it is turned to the unchangeable light of the Word. Let there be light. AUGUSTINE, ibid., chs. 10, 11, 16. If light was made corporeally, etc., up to for there were not yet animals to whom this alternation might be shown.
1.4: 1.4 And God saw the light, etc. STRABO. God made light and darkness, whence Daniel 3: Bless the Lord, light and darkness, when every creature is invited to bless. ISIDORE, on Genesis, ch. 2. Each person has in his works and upright life six distinct days, after which he may hope for rest: on the first day, the light of faith, since first he believes in things invisible, on account of which faith the Lord deigned to appear. And there was evening. AUGUSTINE, On Genesis against the Manichees, bk. 1, ch. 4; BEDE, in the Hexameron. As the light gradually set, and after a space of divine length passed to the lower parts, evening came, as now happens by the customary circuit of the sun. And morning came when the same light returned over the earth and began another day, and one day of twenty-four hours was completed. It must be noted that the night in those first three days was altogether dark, whereas after the stars were created it shone with some light: it was fitting also that days begin from light and extend to the morning of the following day, so that the works of God might be signified as begun from light and completed in light.
1.5: 1.5 And there was evening, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 8, ch. 6, vol. 1. Sin is by no means abandoned in this life through the exercise of righteousness in such a way that one remains in righteousness unshaken: because if uprightness drives out the fault, the fault, sitting at the doors of our thought, knocks to be let in. Hence Moses says: Light was made; and a little after: There was evening. For the Creator, foreknowing human fault, then expressed in time what is now turned over in the mind. For the shadow of temptation follows the light of uprightness. But because the light of the elect is not extinguished by temptation, it is recorded not as night but as evening, because temptation hides the light of righteousness but does not destroy it. AUGUSTINE, On Genesis according to the letter, bk. 4, chs. 22, 23, vol. 3, cols. 311, 312. It must be noted that the other creatures, etc., up to so that the one belongs to the day, the other to the evening.
1.6: 1.6 Let there be a firmament, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 27, ch. 24. The angelic powers, which stood firm in the love of God, received this in recompense: that they remain in the contemplation of the Creator in perpetual happiness, and subsist eternally in that for which they were made. Hence in Moses heaven is said to have been made, and the same is afterward called the firmament, because the angelic nature was first created subtle in the higher places, and afterward, so that it could never fall, was more wondrously confirmed. Let there be a firmament, etc. AUGUSTINE, On Genesis according to the letter, bk. 2, ch. 2, col. 264. It is asked whether that heaven which exceeds the spaces of the air is now being made, etc., up to because its interval divides between certain vapors of waters and the waters that are on the earth. Let there be a firmament, etc. AUGUSTINE, ibid., ch. 4. It must be noted that the firmament is not so called on account of standing still, etc., up to but however they are there, we do not doubt that they are there. Let there be a firmament in the midst. BEDE, in the Hexameron, vol. 2. Of the heaven in which the stars are fixed, etc., up to What kind they are, and for what useful, He knows who made them.
1.7: 1.7 And God made the firmament, etc. AUGUSTINE, On Genesis according to the letter, bk. 2, ch. 8, col. 269. It is asked why, when it had said: Let there be a firmament, and it was so, it afterward adds: And God made the firmament, etc., up to saying: And God said, let there be, etc. Ibid., chs. 1, 3, 5. Above the air is pure fire, etc., up to So the nearness of the supercelestial waters makes it cold. Ibid. It must be noted that on the first day when light was made, it was said only: Let there be light, and this in the word, and there was light, in the work, and at once the created light clung to the uncreated light, as being nearer and more receptive than every creature. On the second day there is a certain delay, and a multiplication of words, let there be, and God made, and it was so: that we may understand that these natures are prone to failing and less apt to obey. JEROME, bk. 1 against Jovinian, vol. 2, col. 211. It must also be noted that the works of this second day are not said, according to the Hebrews, to be good, although they are good like the rest: this is done on account of the number two, the prince of alternation, which is the first to depart from unity: and it is placed in the figure of digamy and of many reprehensible things; hence the creatures that enter the ark by twos are unclean, the odd number clean. Or they are not said to be good for this reason, that in this work the separation of the water is not made perfect, which is made in the next, where it says: Let the waters be gathered together, as will be said there. AUGUSTINE, as above, ch. 9. It is customary to ask of what shape the heaven is: but the Holy Spirit, although our authors knew, did not wish to teach through them anything except what profits salvation. It is also asked whether heaven stands still or moves. If it moves, they say, how is it a firmament? If it stands, how do the stars fixed in it go around? But the firmament can be so called not on account of standing but on account of firmness, or the impassable boundary of the waters. But if it stands, nothing prevents the stars from moving and going around. On the second day was made, as it were, the firmament of discipline, which distinguishes between the carnal and the spiritual, as between the lower and the upper waters. ISIDORE, on Genesis, ch. 2, vol. 5, col. 213. On the second day He set the firmament, that is, the holy Scriptures in the Church. Of these it is said in Isaiah 34: The heaven shall be folded like a book. By this firmament He separates the upper waters, that is, the people of the angels, who have no need to hear the word of God in reading. But He set that firmament over the weakness of the lower peoples, so that looking up to it they may know how He distinguishes between the carnal and the spiritual, as between upper and lower waters. And He divided the waters that were, etc. AMBROSE, Hexameron, bk. 2, ch. 3, vol. 1, col. 148. When you hear this, why do you wonder if a wave could be suspended above the firmament? etc., up to the Jordan also, its river turned back, returns to its source.
1.8: 1.8 And there was evening, etc. ISIDORE, as above. The morning of the second day begins from Noah, etc., up to because boyhood is not suited to generation.
4.9: 4.9 And the Lord said to Cain. ISIDORE, as above. The Lord questions Cain, not as ignorant that He may learn, but as judge that He may punish. To this day the Jews, when we question them through the Scriptures about Christ, answer that they do not know what we are saying. The ignorance of Cain was a lie, the denial of the Jews is false: they would truly be the keepers of Christ if they believed with the heart and confessed with the mouth.
4.10: 4.10 The voice of blood, etc. Great is the power of justice, which demands vengeance for the blood of the innocent.
4.11: 4.11 Now therefore you shall be cursed, etc. RABANUS. It must be noted that in the sin of Adam the earth is cursed. But Cain is cursed, because knowing the condemnation of the first transgression he added fratricide. Now therefore you shall be cursed, etc. By the place, the things that are in the place are signified; as if: you shall be cursed by those who are upon the earth, who have opened their mouth in the confession of sins to receive the blood, which was shed for the remission of their sins, from the hand of the persecutor, who would not be under grace but under the law, so that he is cursed by the Church: which understands and shows him to be cursed: for those who are of the works of the law are under a curse.
4.12: 4.12 When you shall have worked, etc. The relation is to the sound, not to the sense, because earth is understood in one way here, in another above: there for the Church, here for the earthly work which the Jew still practices; that is, carnal circumcision, the passover, the sabbath, and the like, which have a hidden power of understanding the grace of God, but give the Jews no fruit while they refuse to pass over to Christ. In the earth the flesh of Christ can be understood, in which the Jews by crucifying worked our salvation. For He died for our offenses, and rose for our justification: because they denied Him, they were not justified. A wanderer and a fugitive, etc. ISIDORE. Scattered among the nations, a fugitive from Jerusalem. The Seventy: groaning and trembling. Groaning, in sorrow for the lost kingdom; trembling, at the multitude of the Christian people, lest you be killed. My iniquity is greater, etc. He exaggerates the guilt, but confesses proudly, and does not ask for pardon.
4.13: 4.13 My iniquity is greater. ISIDORE. Adding sins to sins he despairs, and does not believe he can obtain pardon, which is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which is forgiven neither in this age nor in the next: because he thinks that God either is unwilling to forgive or is unable, as though He either could not do all things or begrudged salvation. He does not think God angry with him a grave thing, but fears lest he be found and killed.
4.14: 4.14 Everyone therefore that finds me, etc. STRABO. Because from the trembling of the body and the agitation of the frenzied mind, whoever finds me will recognize me as guilty of death.
4.15: 4.15 It shall not be so. That is, you shall not die quickly as you wish, as a remedy for your torment, but it will be punished impersonally: that is, punishment will be taken of you sevenfold, because you will live in torment until the seventh generation, in which you will be killed by Lamech; therefore whoever kills you (understand) will free you from that torment of an evil conscience. This sense appears more clearly. According to the Seventy: Whoever kills Cain shall pay seven vengeances, that is, whoever kills you in the seventh generation will release you by death from torment, you who until that time are to be reserved in life only for punishment, which punishment would soon be ended if you had been killed quickly. So he who would punish the Jews with visible death would take away from them seven vengeances, to which they are bound by the guilt of the killing of Christ, because he would lighten their miseries and dispersions which they suffer. Whoever kills Cain, etc. The Seventy: He shall pay seven vengeances. Aquila, sevenfold; Symmachus, seven times as much; Theodotion, they interpret by a week; in which it is signified that he will be punished long and completely, lest anyone dare to repeat murder. Whoever kills Cain, etc. JEROME, Letter to Damasus. If anyone kills you he shall be punished sevenfold, that is, he shall be punished with the gravest vengeance: a man ought not to kill him to whom God reserved life, either for his own punishment or for the correction of others. But whoever kills Cain. ISIDORE, as above. It is to be read by ellipsis, etc., up to and that is fulfilled: Scatter them by your might (Psalm 53). JEROME, as above. What Aquila put as sevenfold, etc., up to and deserved to be absolved. And the Lord set a mark on Cain, etc. ISIDORE, Questions on Genesis, vol. 5. When all the nations subjugated by the Romans passed into their rites, the Jewish nation, whether under pagan or Christian kings, did not give up the sign of circumcision and carnal observance, etc., up to where paradise was planted. He dwelt in the land on the eastern side of Eden. JEROME, as above. The Seventy: He dwelt in the land of Naid; in the Hebrew it is nod, that is, unstable and wavering, and of uncertain seat. It is not the land of Naid, as our common people think, but the sentence of the Lord is fulfilled while he wanders here and there as a fugitive.
4.17: 4.17 And Cain knew his wife. ISIDORE, ibid. Figuratively, the offspring of the impious, seeking a foundation in the very origin of the world, built in this life a city which he called Enoch, which is interpreted dedication, because in the beginnings they dedicate, while in this life which is before them they plant the root of the heart, that here they may flourish to their wish and wither from the future glory. But Abraham dwelt in tents, because the saints know themselves to be guests and pilgrims, awaiting the city that has foundations, whose builder is God. And he built a city, etc. AUGUSTINE, City of God, bk. 15, ch. 8, vol. 7. It is asked with what helpers he built it, if there were no more men than Scripture says. But it must be known that there were then many more, because by living long they could beget more. Nor is it surprising, since the children of Israel are read to have so multiplied in four hundred years that their army could not be numbered.
4.18: 4.18 Moreover Enoch, etc. JEROME. Certain mysteries are not dug out from all these things, nor would they be found unless first certain roots of history were laid; nor would you gather fruit from the branches of trees unless you had first planted the trunks.
4.19: 4.19 Who took two wives, etc. ISIDORE, as above. It must be noted that the generations from Adam through Cain end with the number eleven, in which transgression is signified. For Lamech is the seventh, to whom three sons and one daughter are added, so that the number eleven is completed, by which sin is signified: and the generation is closed by a woman, who was the beginning of sin, through whom came the pleasure of the flesh, which resists the spirit. Hence she is called Naamah, that is, pleasure. In this offspring Lamech first, against custom, against nature, committed adultery through bigamy.
4.20: 4.20 And Adah bore Jabal, etc. JEROME in the Hebrew Questions. From bigamy is born Jabal dwelling in tents, which, being changeable, figure the instability of those who are carried about by every wind of doctrine. Tubal is also born, the inventor of music, etc., up to like Jabal, Tubal and Tubalcain.
4.21: 4.21 And the name of his brother was Jubal. RABANUS. Josephus writes that he inscribed music on two pillars, one of stone, the other of brick, so that one would not be dissolved by the flood, the other would not be destroyed by fire: the two judgments which Adam had foretold would come.
4.22: 4.22 Tubalcain. RABANUS. Who, according to Josephus, practiced warlike things, and fittingly taught the art of the smith; he also invented certain things which pertain to the lust of the eyes.
4.23: 4.23 And Lamech said, etc. RABANUS. The Hebrews say that Lamech by living long incurred dimness of the eyes, and had a young man as guide and director of his way. Practicing hunting, therefore, he shot an arrow where the young man indicated, and by chance killed Cain hidden among the thickets; and this is what he says: I have slain a man to my wound, that is, by the wound which I inflicted I killed not a beast but a man; whence, kindled with fury, he killed the young man. I have slain a man, etc. STRABO. That is Cain: to my wound, because for him I shall be wounded, that is, killed; and a young man to my bruise, because for him also I shall be condemned.
4.24: 4.24 Vengeance shall be given sevenfold, etc. ALCUIN. Allegorically. The sin of Lamech, who is interpreted humbled, signifies the casting down of the human race, which fell when Adam transgressed, and could not rise either by the law, or by circumcision, or by its own justice, until after seventy-seven generations according to Luke Christ, coming into the world, destroyed sin by the shedding of His blood; hence Matthew 18: I say not to you seven times, but seventy times seven, that is, that the Jew is to be received after seventy-seven vengeances, if he repents and seeks the indulgence of Christ. The number seven signifies totality: by which, multiplied by eleven, the seventy-seventh is made, in which every kind of transgression is signified; which nevertheless in the Gospel is commanded to be forgiven the penitent. JEROME, Letter to Damasus. They say that from Adam to Christ there are seventy-seven generations according to Luke. As therefore in the seventh generation the sin of Cain was loosed (for God will not judge twice for the same thing, and he who has once received in his life will not suffer the same torments in death which he suffered in his life): so also the sin of Lamech, that is, of the whole world, will be loosed by the coming of Christ. A certain Hebrew told me that seventy-seven souls came out of Lamech, who all perished in the flood.
4.25: 4.25 And Adam also knew, etc. Through Seth, who is interpreted resurrection, the life of Christ from the dead is signified: which is signified in the words of the mother: The Lord has given me another seed; as if the Church were to say: I who bore grief for the dead one, rejoice over the one raised.
4.26: 4.26 Whom he called Enos, etc. Enos is interpreted man: who began to call upon the name of the Lord, because through the death of Christ, which Abel signified, and through the resurrection, which Seth signifies, man comes to confess the Lord as Creator and restorer of lost life. JEROME. Whom he called Enos. Enos is interpreted man, who began to call upon the name of the Lord: as Adam is interpreted man, so also Enos, according to the Hebrew truth, is man, or husband; and beautifully, because he had this name, it was said that then was the beginning of calling upon the name of the Lord: although most of the Hebrews think that then first idols were fashioned in the name of the Lord and in His likeness.
5.1: 5.1 This is the book of the generation of Adam. He was made in the likeness of God. Others: in the likeness of Adam. It is as it were a conclusion from the preceding with recapitulation. In the day that God created man. For he was created in the day, because he was established in the brightness of divine contemplation. In the likeness of God. Because He gave him reason, by which by understanding he could discern good and evil, love what he understood, and not hand over to oblivion what he loved, and in this retain the likeness of God. But after through disobedience he destroyed this likeness, being made earthly he begot earthly ones. Hence as is the earthly, such also are the earthly. CHRYSOSTOM, Homily 21 on Genesis, vol. 4. Consider how he used the same words as at the beginning, to teach us that he does not deign to remember thereafter those generations, as having been made reprobate; but begins the genealogy from Seth, who was now born to them, that from this you may learn how great account God takes of the human race, and how He turns away from those whose mind is bloodthirsty.
5.3: 5.3 And Adam lived, etc. JEROME, in the Hebrew Questions. It must be known that up to the flood, where in our manuscripts someone is said to have begotten at two hundred and some years, the Hebrew has one hundred years and the remaining ones that follow. And he begot, etc. As though he too bore the image of the earthly, he who was put in place of the just Abel, and by the interpretation of his name signifies Christ. But all first bear the image of the earthly man before the heavenly, although many before the coming of Christ had through faith the same grace by which Christians are saved. STRABO. They say that after the death of Abel Adam vowed that he would not know his wife any more nor beget a son. But at God's command he broke the vow, that the Son of God might be born of him, and man be redeemed; for He ought not to be born of the stock of Cain. Hence before Seth he is read to have begotten no one, but after him it is said that he begot sons and daughters. This computation of genealogies, as it were, spreads the branches of histories, from which in their places the fruits of mysteries are gathered. And it must be noted that in the generation of Seth no woman is named, as in the generation of Cain: for it belongs to the just to do all things manfully, to assume nothing womanish, nothing fragile. This generation also proceeds by ten up to Noah, in whom the fulfillment of the commandments is signified, as by eleven in the generation of Cain, transgression. In the generation of the unjust Enoch is put first, who is interpreted dedication, because the reprobate in the present life fix the root of their hope, and wither from the love of the unfading inheritance. Of whom it is said in Job 5: I have seen a fool with firm root, and immediately I cursed his beauty. In the generation of the just Enoch is put seventh from Adam, because they do not seek a lasting city here, but extend their expectation to the end of time, which is closed by the sevenfold revolution, when the eighth, eternity, shall have succeeded. Hence this Enoch who is put seventh, and was translated because he pleased God, signifies the seventh rest, to which after this life he who perseveringly clings to God is transferred without delay. The interpretation of the names of this generation also signifies the same: Adam is interpreted man or red earth; Seth, position or resurrection; Enos, man; Cainan, lamentation; Malalehel, praising God; Jared, strengthened; Enoch, dedication; Methuselah, sending forth of death; Lamech, humbled; Noah, rest. Man, therefore, proceeding from the earth, rising again from sins, will be a man calling upon God and weeping for his former sins: and so praising God, strengthened by the Spirit of God, he is dedicated to eternal life. And as victor over death, subject to God, he possesses everlasting rest, which Noah signifies, who is interpreted rest, and is counted in the tenth place, because by the fulfillment of the commandments the kingdom of heaven is possessed.
5.24: 5.24 And Enoch walked with God, etc. ISIDORE, on Genesis. Enoch, the seventh from Adam, pleasing God, etc., up to for three times four make it. ALCUIN. Enoch is preserved from death for so long a time, in which it is shown that man would always have lived if he had not sinned.
5.25: 5.25 And Methuselah lived, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked how Methuselah, according to the computation of years, could have lived after the flood, since all perished except those who entered the ark. But the faultiness of the manuscripts gave rise to this question: for not only is it found otherwise in the Hebrew, but even in the interpretation of the Seventy, in a few manuscripts Methuselah is found to have died seven years before the flood. That the years of Methuselah according to the Seventy are counted beyond the flood is because he signifies Christ, whose life feels no age, so that even in his elders he would seem not to have felt the flood.
5.31: 5.31 And all the days were, etc. JEROME, in the Hebrew Questions, vol. 3. And all the days of Methuselah which he lived were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died. According to careful reckoning he is reported to have lived fourteen years after the flood, etc., up to namely in that year in which the flood began. But Noah, when he was five hundred years old, etc. Ibid. Noah is interpreted rest, because under him all the former works ceased through the flood.
6.1: 6.1 And when men had begun to be multiplied upon the earth. JEROME, in the Hebrew Questions. The Hebrew word Elohim is of both numbers: for it signifies God and gods: therefore Aquila dared to say sons of the gods, understanding holy gods or angels, and following him Symmachus says: The sons of the mighty, seeing the daughters of men.
6.2: 6.2 The sons of God seeing, etc. STRABO. By the sons of God are understood the religious sons of Seth, who, overcome by desire, took wives from the daughters of men, that is, from the stock of Cain, and begot powerful men, huge in body, proud in strength, unruly in manners, who are called giants. It is not incredible that men of this sort were begotten by men, not by angels or certain demons who are wicked toward women, because even after the flood bodies not only of men but also of women have appeared of incredible size.
6.3: 6.3 And God said: My spirit shall not remain, etc. JEROME, ibid. Hebrew loiadon. My spirit shall not judge men forever, for they are flesh. That is, because the condition of men is fragile, etc., up to but of those whom He was going to destroy by the flood. And his days shall be, etc. STRABO. Before the flood, namely for doing penance. But because they persevered in malice before the appointed term, they were destroyed in the hundredth year.
6.5: 6.5 And the Lord seeing, etc. Repentance does not fall upon God, nor sorrow of heart, for whom there is, concerning all things, as fixed a decree as certain foreknowledge: but Scripture uses customary words, adapting itself to our littleness, that from things known we may know the unknown. For the wrath of God is not a disturbance of mind, but the judgment imposed on the sinner: and the thought of His heart is the unchangeable plan of things to be changed.
6.6: 6.6 It repented Him that, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 5. Very often in the sacred word the wise draw God's counsel from the wise of the world. So now, for the benefit of man, the Maker of men Himself takes on a voice of human passion, although it is established that He who beholds all things before they come has done nothing that He should repent. As it is therefore no wonder if the spiritual often use the words of the carnal, so neither is it to be wondered at if the Creator of all Himself, to draw flesh to His understanding, keeps or assumes in Himself the speech of the flesh.
6.9: 6.9 Noah a just man. By his acts he signifies Christ, who says in Matthew 11: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart. He alone is found just, to whom, on account of his justice, seven persons are given. Christ also is just and perfect, to whom the seven Churches, enlightened by the sevenfold Spirit, are granted as one Church. Noah is delivered through water and wood, and his household; so the household of Christ through baptism and the cross. In his generations. As though of justice not completed, but according to his generation.
6.13: 6.13 I will destroy them with, etc. The teachers hand down that the greenness and fertility of the earth was far inferior after the flood; and therefore the eating of flesh was granted to men, whereas before they lived only on the fruits of the earth.
6.14: 6.14 Make for yourself an ark of wood. That is, strong and indissoluble, and well joined; which another translation says squared, so that it would not be broken either by the force of winds or by flood. Little rooms, etc. STRABO. The Seventy: You shall make rooms with two stories and three stories in the ark: two-storied in the lower parts, three-storied in the upper. It was therefore divided into five dwellings: the first, that is the lowest, was for dung, where the dung drained away, so that those in the ark would not be hurt by the stench; the second, a storehouse; the third, for wild animals and serpents; the fourth, for tame ones; the fifth, that is the highest, for men and birds. The door, where the two-storied and three-storied were joined, that is, between the storehouse and the dwelling of the beasts. AUGUSTINE. In the first dwelling in the lower parts the ark was single-storied, in the second above the lower dwelling two-storied. In the third, above the second, three-storied. Others say that in the lower parts there were two little rooms, and so the ark was two-storied. Of these the lower received the dung, the second the food, which was called the storehouse; in the upper parts it was three-storied, where men and animals were contained in suitable distinction. ISIDORE, on Genesis, vol. 5. Noah built the ark of incorruptible wood, etc., up to prophesied in five, evangelized in the sixth.
6.15: 6.15 Of three hundred cubits, etc. ISIDORE, ibid. In the three hundred cubits the wood of the cross can be shown, etc., up to because there is one God from whom are all things, and one faith, and one baptism. GREGORY, Homily 16 on Ezekiel. The ark which was commanded to be made three hundred cubits in length, fifty in breadth, thirty in height, etc., up to and through whom all advance who know themselves to be sinners.
6.16: 6.16 In a cubit you shall finish its top. So the Church, gathered in unity, is raised on high and perfected; hence Matthew 11: He who does not gather with me scatters. And the door of the ark, etc. For no one enters the Church except through the sacrament of the remission of sins, which flowed from the opened side. Upper rooms and third stories, etc. The Seventy: Two-storied and three-storied. For from all nations the Church gathers either a twofold multitude, from the circumcision and the uncircumcision; or a threefold, from the three sons of Noah, by whose offspring the world is filled. The lower parts of the ark are divided, because in this earthly life there is diversity of nations: but at the top all are consummated into one, because Christ is all and in all. ALCUIN. Fittingly the ark was peaked at the top, like a narrow roof, to shed the threats of the rains, and the lowest part, standing squared in the waters with stability, could be neither tilted nor sunk by the push of winds, nor by the force of waves, nor by the restlessness of the animals within. GREGORY in the Moralia. The ark, wide in the lower parts, narrow in the upper, etc., up to great heaps of chaff, which are burned with fires. GREGORY. Morally, he who turns from love of the world builds in his heart an ark of salvation, having in himself length, that is, faith in the Trinity, and length of life and immortality; breadth in charity, by which he can do good even to enemies; height in hope, by which he lifts himself to heavenly things and refers the sum of his acts to the One.
6.19: 6.19 And of all, etc. AUGUSTINE, City of God, bk. 15, last chapter, vol. 7. It is asked about the very tiny creatures; so good and bad are mingled in the sacraments of the Church.
6.21: 6.21 You shall therefore take, etc. It is usual to ask about animals that are thought to eat only flesh, whether they were there beyond the number without transgression of the command, having been shut in by the necessity of feeding others; or, which is rather to be believed, there could be foods besides flesh that suited all. For many animals whose food is flesh feed on fruits and apples, especially figs and chestnuts. The just and wise man, divinely admonished, could therefore find and store for each the food that suited it, besides flesh. And hunger compels all to eat, and there is nothing that God cannot make sweet and wholesome, who would even grant by divine power that they live without food.
7.1: 7.1 And the Lord said, etc. Of all clean animals you shall take seven and seven, etc. RABANUS. We must understand not seven doubled, that is fourteen, but only seven. Likewise two and two, not four, but only two, a male and a female. And it must be noted that the clean animals are brought in by an odd number, that is seven, the unclean by an even; because an odd number portends the look of strength, an even one infirmity. The clean are more numerous, that Noah on coming out of the ark might have something to sacrifice and eat. ISIDORE, on Genesis. Of all animals, etc. Not that there are more good than evil, etc., up to which day, the third from the passion, in the number of days that roll through all time, is both first and eighth. AUGUSTINE on Genesis. It is asked whether so great an ark could be built in a hundred years by four men, that is, Noah and his three sons. But if it could not, it was no great matter to employ other craftsmen, although, having obtained the wages of their work, they did not care whether Noah acted wisely or foolishly, and did not enter into it, because they did not believe what he believed.
7.4: 7.4 I will rain, etc. ISIDORE, Questions on Genesis, ch. 7. Because every guilt is committed against the Decalogue throughout the whole world, which is divided into four parts: and four times ten make forty; whether guilt is contracted from prosperity, which pertains to the days; or from adversity, which pertains to the nights, it is washed away in baptism.
7.5: 7.5 Noah therefore did all things, etc. And he was six hundred years old, etc. ISIDORE, ibid. Noah was five hundred years old when the Lord commanded him to make the ark, etc., up to which is the square of three.
7.7: 7.7 Noah and his sons, his wife, etc. went in. RABANUS. It must be noted that Noah enters the ark separately with his sons, and their wives separately. Therefore it is said distinctly: Noah and his sons went in, and distinctly added, his wife and the wives of his sons. But the men went out mixed with the women, for so it is written: Noah went out and his wife. For there is a time of embracing and a time of refraining from embraces (Ecclesiasticus 3).
7.10: 7.10 And when they had passed, etc. ISIDORE. Because we are baptized in hope of the future rest, which the seventh day signifies, all flesh outside the ark was consumed by the flood; because outside the Church the water of baptism, although it is the same, avails not for salvation but for destruction.
7.11: 7.11 In the six hundredth year, etc. Allegorically. It must be noted that in the six hundredth year the waters of the flood overflowed, because in the sixth age of the world the sacrament of baptism was first commended, and this on the seventeenth day of the second month, because ten signifies the Decalogue. Seven, on account of the Sabbath, signifies the seventh rest, and because in the Decalogue the renunciation of vices is seen, whoever is initiated in baptism professes, for the sake of eternal rest, to renounce all vices. The floodgates. Windows, that is, clouds, which were opened so that unusual and greater rains might be poured out from them. Cataracts properly are the mouths of the Nile, but are used loosely for all windows. RABANUS. About the ark it is usual to ask whether with so great a capacity as is described it could carry all the animals said to have entered, and their foods? Origen solves this by the geometric cubit, asserting that it is not said in vain that Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, who loved geometry, and that the geometric cubit contains as much as six of ours.
7.15: 7.15 Two and two, etc. AUGUSTINE, as above. Above He commanded that seven and seven of the clean be taken, two and two of the unclean. How then does it now say that two and two entered, whether of the clean or the unclean? But this refers not to the number of the clean and unclean, but to male and female. For in all there are two, male and female. It must be noted, however, that what is said, in which was the spirit of life, is said not only of men but also of cattle: because some wish that what is written, He breathed into his face the spirit of life, be understood of the Holy Spirit; but some manuscripts have better, the breath of life.
7.17: 7.17 Forty days, etc. ALCUIN. The rain flooded for the number forty, which shows the tribulation of penance. After forty days Noah opened the window, signifying that heaven is opened to those who fast. Hence Moses, Elijah, and the Savior Himself consecrated fasts by the number forty, as necessary in three times, before the law, under the law, under grace.
7.20: 7.20 Fifteen cubits higher, etc. AUGUSTINE on Genesis. If the earth of Mount Olympus, as history relates, could invade the space of the calm air, etc., up to to hold fast rest and faith in the resurrection. Fifteen. There are those who think that neither the quality of the earth nor the height of the mountains before the flood was such as it is today.
7.23: 7.23 They were destroyed from the earth. ALCUIN. Land animals perished rather than aquatic ones, because they live from the cursed earth.
8.1: 8.1 And God remembered Noah, etc. He brought a spirit upon the earth, etc. ALCUIN, Questions on Genesis. This can be understood of that spirit of which it was said, The Spirit of God moved over the waters: then it moved, so that, the waters being gathered into their place, the earth might appear: now it is brought, so that, the waters of the flood being taken away, it might reveal the face of the earth. By spirit a wind can be understood, according to Psalm 106: And the spirit of the storm stood, by whose blasts, that is, the water receded.
8.4: 8.4 And the ark rested in the seventh month, etc. ISIDORE. It signifies the sevenfold rest, and because the perfect rest there, the number of the above-mentioned square is repeated. For on the twenty-seventh day of the second month the sacrament is commended, and again on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month it is confirmed, when the ark rested: for what is promised in hope is shown in fact. AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether these things happened after one hundred and fifty days, or whether by recapitulation all are recalled that began to happen after the forty days of rain, so that only this pertains to the hundred and fifty days, that the water was raised up to the very mountains, either from the fountains of the abyss, the rain now ceasing, or because it remained at its height with no wind drying it. The other things that are said did not all happen after the hundred and fifty days, but are recalled: they began to happen from the end of the forty days.
8.5: 8.5 For in the tenth month. It must be noted that in the tenth month the tops of the mountains appeared, which the waters of the flood had exceeded by fifteen cubits, because the sacraments of eternal rest and the glory of the resurrection, which the wisdom of the proud did not know, the eminence of the saints understood through the fulfillment of the commandments; hence Psalm 118: From Your commandments I have understood. And elsewhere, Luke 10: You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to little ones.
8.7: 8.7 Which went forth, etc. ISIDORE. That after forty days the raven did not return, either caught by the waters or enticed by a floating corpse, figures those most foul with the uncleanness of covetousness: and therefore those too intent on the things which are outside in the world, either to be rebaptized, or to be seduced and held by those whom baptism outside the ark, that is the Church, kills. AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether the raven died, or could somehow live. For if there was land on which it might rest, the dove would likewise have found rest. Hence it is conjectured that the raven could perch on a corpse, which the dove naturally shuns.
8.8: 8.8 He also sent. ISIDORE. The dove sent out, and returning because it found no rest, signifies that through the New Testament rest is not promised to the saints in this world: for it was sent out after forty days, by which number the life lived in the world is designated. STRABO. The ark contains the raven and the dove, and the Church the good and the bad. The raven sent out does not return, because the reprobate, clinging to the allurements of the world, perish. The dove returned, carrying an olive branch with green leaves in its mouth, because the saints, rejoicing in simplicity, carry the gift of peace in their mouth, saying: Psalm 119: With those who hated peace I was peaceable: when I spoke to them, etc.
8.9: 8.9 It returned. AUGUSTINE. The question is how the dove did not find where to rest, since the tops of the mountains were already bare according to the order of the narrative? This can be solved by recapitulation, so that the things done earlier are understood as narrated later, or rather they had not yet dried.
8.10: 8.10 Having waited, etc. After seven other days, the dove sent out on account of the sevenfold spiritual working brought back a fruitful sprig of olive, signifying that many baptized outside the Church, if the fatness of charity is not lacking, are in a later time brought back in the mouth of the dove, as in the kiss of peace, to the fellowship of unity.
8.11: 8.11 Carrying a branch. ALCUIN. The dove brings an olive branch to Noah after the flood, the foul bird having been driven out, because the dove of the Holy Spirit, coming to Christ after baptism, announces peace with the branch of refreshment and light.
8.12: 8.12 And he waited nevertheless other seven days, etc. ISIDORE on Genesis. The dove sent out after another seven days, and not returning, signifies the end of the age, when there will be the rest of the saints, not in the sacrament of hope, by which the Church is now joined together, as long as that is drunk which flowed from the side of Christ, but in the perfection of salvation, when the kingdom shall be handed over to God and the Father, so that in that clear contemplation of truth we need no mysteries.
8.13: 8.13 In the six hundred and first year, etc. Ibid. Of the life of Noah, that is, six hundred years having been completed, the roof of the ark is opened, etc., up to one being added, on account of the bond of unity.
8.14: 8.14 In the second month. STRABO. Historically. That is, May; Noah made a year in the ark, and went out on the very day on which he had entered. For he entered on the twenty-seventh day of the second month; now he says that he went out on the twenty-seventh day of the same month. But it must be known that if eleven are added to the present day, as the moon is today, so it will be after a year on the same day. When Noah entered, it was the seventeenth moon, or the seventeenth day of the second month. Therefore after a year, eleven having been added, it was the twenty-seventh day and the seventeenth moon. In the second month, etc. Mystically. As was said above, on the seventeenth day of the six hundredth year the earth was drenched with the waters of the flood, but on the twenty-seventh day of the second month it was dried, when it was commanded that they go out of the ark, and receive a covenant that they would no more perish by the waters of the flood. In this it can be understood that by seventeen, as above, the state of beginners can be signified, when vices are renounced; by twenty-seven the advancement of the perfect in the consummation of virtues. For if you add ten to seventeen, it makes twenty-seven. If to the ten precepts by which sins are renounced you add evangelical perfection, by which it is commanded not only not to be angry but even to love enemies, and the like, you have come to that age of perfection in which you do not need the aforesaid sacraments; and going out of the ark, that is, coming from hope to sight, you will find the rest promised in the sacraments.
8.15: 8.15 Go out of the ark, etc. ISIDORE. They go out joined, who entered separated, because now the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh. But in the resurrection of the just the body will cling to the spirit in perfect peace, no need of change or concupiscence resisting.
8.20: 8.20 And taking, etc. AUGUSTINE. Clean and unclean animals entered the ark, but after the exit only the clean are offered to God. But what He says: I will not strike every living soul as I have done, and added what goodness bestows with generosity on the unworthy, perhaps the indulgence of the New Testament is figured, so that the past vengeance pertains to the severity of the law, this to the goodness of grace.
8.21: 8.21 For the sense, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 38. Let no one take credit for himself if he has conquered his thoughts: because the evil of corruption, which each person took from the origin of carnal desires, exercises itself as age advances: and unless the hand of divine strength restrains this quickly, the fault devours every good of nature into the depth; Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase (1 Corinthians 3).
9.1: 9.1 And God blessed Noah and his sons, etc. Increase and multiply. Man is set over the other animals as a terror, as a comfort after the vengeance now past, and lest the few men be overwhelmed by the many beasts, and that they may know that they rule over the irrational but not over the rational.
9.2: 9.2 And the fear of you, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 2, ch. 11. For powerful men the virtue of humility is great, etc., up to by which they seek not their own glory but the benefit of their subjects.
9.4: 9.4 Flesh with blood. ISIDORE. All animals are given them for food, because in the calling of the nations to the faith there is no distinction, which is figured in the sheet of Peter. They are forbidden to eat blood, lest the former life, as if smothered, be held in the conscience, but be poured out through confession. The eating of flesh seems to have been granted after the flood, on account of the unfruitfulness of the earth and the frailty of man.
9.9: 9.9 Behold I will establish a covenant, etc. God set a covenant between Himself and men and every living soul, that He would not destroy it by a flood, namely the bow which appears in the clouds, which never shines except from the sun. For those do not perish by the flood, separated from the Church, who in the prophets and in all the holy Scriptures, as in the clouds of God, recognize the glory of Christ, and do not seek their own. But lest the worshipers of this sun swell with pride, let them know that Christ is signified by the sun just as by the lion, by the lamb, by the stone, for the sake of likeness, not by property of substance.
9.13: 9.13 I will set my bow, etc. ALCUIN on Genesis. God gave the bow as a sign of security, lest fearful men dread being destroyed by another flood, often seeing floods of rains. It is set in heaven so that it can be seen by all, and in any tribulation we may lift up the eyes of the heart to Him who dwells in the heavens. And because a bow is made only from the rays of the sun and a moist cloud, it seems that before the flood there had been no rains. The earth could have been made fruitful by dew and the overflow of fountains. STRABO. The bow has two colors, blue and fiery, which express two judgments: one of water, which is past; the other of fire, which is believed to come at the end of the age: hence the blue color is outside, the fiery inside.
9.18: 9.18 The sons of Noah therefore were, etc. JEROME in the Hebrew Questions. Often the Seventy, unable to render into Greek the letter heth, because it sounds a double aspiration, added the Greek chi, teaching that in words of this kind there is to be an aspiration. Hence they translated Cham for what is Ham, from whom Egypt is called Ham to this day in the language of the Egyptians.
9.21: 9.21 And drinking wine, etc. Christ also was inebriated, when He suffered; stripped, when crucified. In his tent, that is, among those of the household of His blood, then the mortality of the flesh was laid bare. To the Jews a scandal, to the Gentiles foolishness, but to those called themselves, Jews and Gentiles, as it were Shem and Japheth, the power of God and the wisdom of God: for the foolishness of God is wiser than men. ALCUIN. After the flood Noah was inebriated, because perhaps he did not know that one could be made drunk by wine. For before the flood men are not read to have used wine. Therefore it is said specially of Noah that he planted a vineyard. The uncovering of the thigh follows drunkenness as lust follows satiety.
9.22: 9.22 And when he had seen it, etc. PROCOPIUS on Genesis. From these circumstances the sin of Ham is magnified. He holds his parent in contempt, blurts out how shamefully his father lay, and tells not one of his brothers but both: if more had been at hand, he would have disclosed the deed to all: the deed seemed laughable to him, to whom it least should have; the matter was worthy of shame and caution, lest its infamy spread to others: nor does he tell it to those who were of the household, but to outsiders. ISIDORE. The Jews, seeing the death of Christ, mocked. But Shem and Japheth, the two peoples believing from the uncircumcision and the circumcision, turned away and covered, etc., up to as if meeting in peace in the corner.
9.23: 9.23 But Shem, etc. GREGORY in the Moralia. We are said to turn away from what we disapprove. What is it then that the sons covered their father's nakedness, coming backward with cloaks thrown over their shoulders, unless that to good subjects the evils of their superiors so displease that they hide them from the knowledge of others: they carry the covering turned away, because, while judging the deed and venerating the master, they do not wish to see what they cover.
9.24: 9.24 Cursed be Canaan, a servant, etc. Ibid. God does not leave sins unpunished, but judgment so begins in our correction that it rests in the condemnation of the reprobate. For judgment begins at the house of God. What then is the end of those who have not believed, who do not feel temporal scourges? For they will perish forever; their wickedness was figured in Ham sinning. To whom it is said: Cursed be Canaan, a servant, etc. The father sinning, the son received the sentence, because the wickedness of the reprobate long prospers here, but perishes hereafter.
9.26: 9.26 Blessed be the Lord God of Shem. Although He is the God of all nations, as by a proper name He is called also among the nations themselves the God of Israel, which comes from the blessing of Japheth, because among the people of the nations the Church has occupied the circle of the earth, which was foretold when it was said: May God enlarge Japheth. Canaan. STRABO. From whom come the Canaanites, who by this curse are prophesied to be driven out of their place of habitation.
9.27: 9.27 May God enlarge Japheth, etc. JEROME. Of Shem the Hebrews, of Japheth the Gentiles. Since therefore the multitude of believers has been broad, from the breadth which is called Japheth, breadth is named. And what it says: And let him dwell in the tents of Shem, is prophesied of us who, Israel having been cast out, dwell in the learning and knowledge of the Scriptures. May God enlarge Japheth, etc. ISIDORE. Shem the elder, he is the Jewish people, from whom came the patriarchs, and prophets, and apostles, etc., up to that is, their work.
10.1: 10.1 These are the generations, etc. The two sons of Noah having been blessed, and the middle one cursed, their generations are woven, from whom seventy-two nations arose: fifteen from Japheth, thirty from Ham, twenty-seven from Shem. To these the Lord sent seventy-two disciples. Shem. ALCUIN. Shem, as they think, obtained Asia; Ham Africa; Japheth Europe. Japheth. The younger son, from whom were born seven sons, who held the northern region from the Taurus and Amanus, mountains of Cilicia and Syria, to the river Tanais, and in Europe as far as Gadira. They left their names to places and nations, of which very many have been changed, the rest remain.
