10.2: 10.2 Gomer. These are the Galatians, according to Josephus, who are called in Latin Gallogreeks. Tubal. The Iberians, who are also the Spaniards, from whom Celtiberia, although some suspect the Italians. Canaan. He obtained the land which the Jews afterward possessed, the Canaanites having been cast out.
10.8: 10.8 Regma and Saba, etc. JEROME. Gradually they lost the ancient names, and what they now have in place of the old ones is unknown. Saba. Different from the one above, and they differ in writing: for that one is written with samech, this with shin; for where we say: The kings of the Arabs and of Saba shall bring gifts, in the Hebrew it is scheba and seba. Nimrod. Who wished to penetrate heaven beyond nature. He signifies the devil, who said: I will ascend above the stars of heaven. Nimrod, according to Josephus, seized tyranny from a new desire of kingship, and was the author of building the tower that would touch heaven. He began to be mighty, or a giant, according to others. But Scripture has recorded giants born before. But perhaps after the flood the newness of the human race being restored is recalled, because he began to be a giant on the earth.
10.9: 10.9 A mighty hunter. ALCUIN. That is, an oppressor and destroyer of men, whom he enticed to build a tower against God.
10.10: 10.10 Babylon. It is confusion, because there the division of tongues was made.
10.11: 10.11 Asshur. The empire of the Assyrians, which was first under Ninus, who built Nineveh, which on account of its repentance is called beautiful.
10.13: 10.13 But Mizraim, etc. JEROME. Except the Laabim, from whom the Libyans were afterward named, who were formerly called Phutaeans, and the Casluhim, who were afterward called Philistim, whom we corruptly call Palestinians, the other six nations are unknown to us, because they were overthrown in the Ethiopian war. They possessed the land from Gaza to the farthest bounds of Egypt. Ludim and Anamim. Laabim, Naphtuhim, etc. All these are unknown, either because the nations were destroyed in the Ethiopian war, or because it is not known what names they now have.
10.21: 10.21 Of Shem. He speaks of him last, because he pursues his generation and the line of the generation. Eber. Who is fifth from Shem, son of Noah. Is it because the Hebrews are said to be named from him, or because through him the generation passes to Abraham? Which then is more probable, that they are called Hebrews as Eberites, or as Abrahamites, is rightly asked.
10.25: 10.25 And to Eber were born sons, etc. Eber, a passer-over, from whom the Hebrews, that is, passers-over. The true Hebrews are those who pass from present things to future, from perishable to lasting. These nations from the river Cono possessed all the region that is called Geria.
11.1: 11.1 And the earth was of one lip, etc. AUGUSTINE, on Genesis. It was said above that the sons of Noah, or of his sons, were distributed through the lands according to their tongues. But this he recalls afterward by recapitulation, what was earlier. But the obscurity is caused by his weaving in that kind of speech, as if the narrative followed of things that were done afterward.
11.2: 11.2 And as they journeyed. CHRYSOSTOM, on Genesis. See how the human race cannot remain within its bounds, but desiring more, always seeks greater things. And this is what destroys the human race, that it will not recognize the measure of its nature, but always desires greater. Because they saw, he says, a plain in the land of Shinar, migrating and leaving the former place, they dwelt there.
11.3: 11.3 Come. They feared the flood again; therefore, with Nimrod as author, they wished to build themselves a tower in which they would not fear a flood. A foolish and impious boldness, whence followed vengeance and the division of tongues. ISIDORE on Genesis. The tower is the pride of the world, or the dogmas of heretics, etc., up to the unity of confession and faith.
11.7: 11.7 Come therefore, etc. It is understood to have been said to the angels; or according to that: Let us make man in our image and likeness. For in the singular number is added: and He divided them, etc., as there: God made man in His image and likeness. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 2, ch. 5. Come, etc. It is said to those who cling to God, Come, because never to fall away from divine contemplation, but always to increase, and never to withdraw in heart, is by a steady motion always to come. The angels ascend by beholding the Creator, they descend by pressing down with the rigor of judgment the creature unlawfully exalting itself. To say, therefore, Let us go down, and confound their tongue, is to show in Himself what is rightly done, and by the force of inner vision to inspire by hidden movements the judgments to be displayed to their minds.
11.8: 11.8 He divided them. ALCUIN. In this division of tongues God made nothing new, but divided the manners of speaking and the forms of speech among different nations. Hence we find the same syllables and letters of the same power joined otherwise in different languages, and often the same names or words signifying something else; hence where it is said in Psalm 2: With a rod of iron, in the Greek it reads, in raudo sidera. In Latin, therefore, sidera does not signify iron, as in Greek, but stars. AUGUSTINE, City of God, bk. 16, ch. 4. Rightly is an evil intention punished, even when the effect does not follow. What kind of punishment was it? For since the dominion of the one commanding is in language, there pride was condemned, so that the one giving orders was not understood by man, who refused to understand so as to obey God commanding.
11.10: 11.10 Shem was a hundred years old. BEDE, Hexameron, bk. 3, vol. 2, col. 131. A great question arises for us according to the letter, how Shem is said to be a hundred years old two years after the flood, when above he is asserted to have been born in the five hundredth year of Noah, and the flood is read to have come in the six hundredth year of the same Noah, etc., up to because God took him.
11.26: 11.26 Terah begot Abram and Nahor. AUGUSTINE, Question 25 on Genesis. Not at the same time, but in their own times, from when he began to beget. Nor is the order of birth to be attended to in these, but the signification of future dignity, in which Abram excels.
11.31: 11.31 In Ur of the Chaldeans. JEROME. In the Hebrew, in Ur Chesdim, that is, in the fire of the Chaldeans. The Hebrews fable here that Abram was cast into the fire, because he would not adore the fire which the Chaldeans worship, and being freed by God's help he escaped from the fire of idolatry. Hence it is said to him: I am He who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans. Haran, father of Milcah. Ibid. The same is father of both. Haran, son of Terah, brother of Abram and Nahor, begot two daughters, Milcah and Sarai, surnamed Iscah. Nahor married Milcah, and Abram Sarai. For marriages between uncles and nieces had not yet been forbidden, which in the beginning were even celebrated between brothers and sisters. Terah therefore took Abram, etc., up to the days of Terah were two hundred and five years, and he died in Haran. AUGUSTINE. It is said first that when Terah was seventy years old he begot Abram, and afterward with all his he remained in Haran, and died. And it was said to Abram that he should go out of Haran, and he went out when he was seventy-five years old. But by recapitulation it is shown that the Lord commanded while the father was alive, etc., up to from whom the Jews are named on account of the royal tribe.
12.1: 12.1 Go out of your land, etc. AUGUSTINE, as above. The account of Stephen on this matter is to be considered, etc., up to so then Abram was settled in that land, when he lived there until the birth of Jacob. STRABO. It must be noted that he had already gone out of his land, but then he had gone out in body, not in mind and will; he perhaps had the mind to return, when it was said to him: Go out, etc. ISIDORE. Christ left the land and kindred of the Jews, and was magnified among the nations. We too must go out from our land, that is, from earthly means and wealth, and from kindred, that is the conversation of vices, which, clinging to us from birth, are joined to us like affinities of blood; and from the house of the father, that is from the memory of the world, that renouncing it we may be enlarged with the people of God, and, when the time comes, be brought into the land of the heavenly promise.
12.2: 12.2 And I will make you a great nation, etc. ISIDORE. Two things are promised to Abram: namely that his seed will possess the land of Canaan, when it is said: And come into the land which I shall show you. But another, far more excellent, not of carnal but of spiritual seed, by which he is to be father not only of the Jewish nation but of all nations following his faith; which is thus promised: And in you all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.
12.4: 12.4 Seventy-five years. JEROME in the Hebrew Questions. If Terah, father of Abram, in the region of Chaldea, etc., up to and stayed there a longer time.
12.8: 12.8 Bethel. RABANUS. It is interpreted house of God, which was afterward called Bethaven, that is house of an idol. Ai. Mystically. Ai is interpreted eye or fountain. The patriarch, therefore, tending to the land of promise, pitched his tent between Bethel and Ai, because the saints, regenerated by the fountain of baptism, being watchful in the course of this life, hasten to the tabernacle of God, that is, the heavenly city.
12.13: 12.13 Say therefore, I beg you, etc. AUGUSTINE, City of God, bk. 16, ch. 19. It is asked why the patriarch wished to lie, etc., up to both his life and the chastity of his wife.
12.15: 12.15 The woman was taken. RABANUS. Sarai is excused, who is carried into the house of Pharaoh unwillingly, not only in this, that neither body nor soul is defiled except by consent of the mind, but also in this, that it was done with her husband agreeing and permitting. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis. She could remain so long untouched with Pharaoh, because in Esther it is read that girls were not brought in to kings at once, but were kept one year, and for six months were anointed with oil of myrrh, and for another six months were among various perfumes. She could therefore remain untouched through this lapse of time. And meanwhile the Egyptians treated Abram well, until Pharaoh, scourged by God and learning that she was his wife, gave her back untouched.
13.1: 13.1 Abram therefore went up, etc. JEROME in the Hebrew Questions. Delivered from Egypt, he is read to have gone up well, but how could he be very rich? But in the Hebrew truth it reads heavy exceedingly: for he was burdened with the weight of Egypt. And although there seem to be riches of gold and silver, yet if they are Egyptian, they are heavy to the holy man; nor, as is read in the Seventy, He went from where he had come into the desert as far as Bethel, but, according to the Hebrew, He went on his journey by the south as far as Bethel. For he set out from Egypt, not to seek the desert, which he had left in Egypt, but to come by the south, which is opposite the north, to the house of God, where his tent was between Bethel and Ai.
13.3: 13.3 To Bethel, etc. Bethel is a small city at the twelfth milestone from Aelia, on the right as one goes to Neapolis: it was formerly called Luz, that is Almond, in the tribe of Benjamin: Ai in the tribe of Judah, set apart for the priests; Bethel, house of God; Ai, eye or fountain: well, then, pitching his tent between Bethel and Ai, he built an altar to the Lord, because the saints, withdrawing from the prince of the world and the pleasures of the age, washed in the holy fountain of baptism, carefully conducting the course of the present life, and offering to God the sacrifice of praise and of good work upon the altar of faith, tend happily to the house of God, that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem.
13.6: 13.6 For their substance was great, etc. Let there not be, I beg, etc. Let us too put nothing before concord and charity, but through the right hand of prosperity or the left of adversity persevere in peace and love. The quarrel between the herdsmen of Lot and the herdsmen of Abram signifies controversy between Catholic shepherds and subverting heretics. Hence Lot too signifies heresiarchs, being interpreted turning aside; and he chose for himself the region around the Jordan, that is descent. His herdsmen are heretics and schismatics, who seek what is beautiful and sloping, and do not go up the mountain with Moses to the Lord, holding to peace and unity; and they receive the choice of where they wish to go; and fleeing grace, commit themselves to free will. The herdsmen of Abram signify Catholic teachers, who flee heretics even in place, according to Titus 3: Avoid a heretical man after the first and second admonition: and this among the nations of the Canaanites and Perizzites, in the land of promise, because between Catholics and heretics there is usually contention as to whose is the kingdom of heaven. For we are brothers. In three ways are people called brothers in holy Scripture: by nature, as Jacob and Esau; by kinship, as Abram and Lot; by nation, as all the Jews. Hence if your brother be reduced to poverty and sell himself to you, etc.
13.10: 13.10 Like paradise, etc. From this we learn that there is an earthly paradise, to which the earthly irrigation is compared. For this region was level and flat, and watered by the flowing Jordan, as Egypt by the Nile.
13.13: 13.13 Before the Lord. To whom a crime to be punished is committed: for the crime was manifest also to men, but not to be punished.
13.14: 13.14 Lift up your eyes, etc. As if: look through the four quarters of the world; the possession of Palestine is promised to him and his seed. That in some manuscripts sea is put for west is done because Palestine has the sea on the west.
13.15: 13.15 All the land, etc. Not only this was promised. For it was not said, I will give you as much land as you see; but, I will give you the land which you see. For although the land beyond on every side was also given, this was chiefly given which was seen. Hence he added: Arise and walk through the land, etc., that is, by walking through it he might reach that which he could not see standing in one place. By it is signified the land which Israel, the seed of Abram according to the flesh, not according to faith, received: which was to be as the sand of the sea, because it cannot be numbered. I will give to you. To Christ is promised the inheritance of all nations, who has spread His Church throughout the whole world, to whom the Father says: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance (Psalm 2). And Psalm 71: And He shall rule from sea to sea.
13.18: 13.18 In Hebron. It is a city in the tribe of Judah, which is also called Kiriath-arba, that is, city of four; for CHARIAT in Hebrew is city, arbe four. For there lie the greatest Adam and Abram, Isaac and Jacob.
14.1: 14.1 Amraphel. Interpreted 'he said that he should fall,' and he is king of Shinar, which is interpreted shaking out of teeth or their stench. He signifies heretics, who tend to a fall, and with guileful words vomit a foul sense. Arioch. Interpreted drunk or drunkenness: he signifies the folly of the Gentiles, who, drunk with iniquity, worship the creature instead of the Creator, and are tossed about by the allurements of the world. Chedorlaomer. Interpreted a comely sheaf, who is king of Elam, that is, of this age: he signifies hypocrisy, which although vain and pernicious, yet seems comely on the surface, but what it was will appear in the future. Tidal. Interpreted knowing the yoke or explorer, who is king of the nations; he signifies avarice, which, shrewd and crafty, subjugates many to itself. Amraphel, etc. These four kings figure the four principal vices, contrary to the four principal virtues; which strive to subjugate the five senses, signified by the five kings, through the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of the world.
14.2: 14.2 Bela. JEROME. In Hebrew it is called devouring. The Hebrews relate that elsewhere it is called Salisa, and 'frightened heifer,' because it was swallowed up by a third earthquake. And from the time when Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim were overthrown by divine fire, that one was called little. For Zoar is translated 'little,' which in the Syriac tongue is called Zoara. The Vale of Salt Pits, in which were the pits of bitumen, after the wrath of God and the rain of sulphur, was turned into the Dead Sea, which by the Greeks is called the lake of Asphalt, that is of bitumen. Mystically. Four kings overcome five, while contrary powers, abusing the five senses of the body, ensnare and capture them with vices. Allegorically. Such kings overcome first Bera, who is interpreted malice or creature, and is king of the Sodomites, that is of blindness, or of a silent beast, when they persuade those who persevere in old malice to follow, in the manner of beasts, the blindness of lust. They conquer also Birsha, that is one placed in narrowness, king of Gomorrah, that is of a swelling and seditious people, when they overwhelm and cast down those who are distressed by the cares of the world and do not fear to commit the wickedness of plunder. They conquer also Shinab, king of Admah, that is, the earthly, when they urge those who relish only earthly things to remain in luxury, so as to say: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die (1 Corinthians 15). They conquer Shemeber, who is interpreted there destruction, and is king of Zeboiim, that is of the girdle of sorrow, when through anger and envy they deceive the unwary; hence Job 5: Anger kills the fool, envy slays the little one. They conquer also the king of Bela, when they cast the fainthearted into despair; for Bela is interpreted headlong fall or swallowing: the devil strives for this above all, that after the fall of sin he may cast into despair.
14.4: 14.4 Twelve, etc. Twelve is a superfluous number. In this superfluity our five senses serve vain superstition, which Chedorlaomer signifies, and the four vices adjoining it; and those wishing to withdraw suffer grievous persecution, and are often overcome.
14.7: 14.7 And they struck. JEROME. Another edition has, etc., up to because there God judged the people. The Rephaim in Ashtaroth, etc. The names of places and nations signify those living carnally, whom vices easily conquer.
14.13: 14.13 The Hebrew. The Seventy: from beyond the river; namely because, coming from Mesopotamia, having crossed the river Euphrates, he set his dwelling in the land of Canaan. Hence Joshua: Why do you wish to serve the gods of your fathers who are beyond the river?
14.14: 14.14 And when Abram heard this, etc. ISIDORE. Mystically. Likewise our faith, when strengthened by the principal Spirit, subjects the five senses of the body, as five kings, triumphing by the word of God over the outer man. He defeated the adversaries with three hundred and eighteen, because we in the sacrament of the cross, which the letter tau signifies, which signifies three hundred, overcome the five carnal senses, which formerly held us captive by various vices. Eighteen, multiplied from three and six, signifies faith in the Trinity and the perfection of works, by which full victory of virtues over vices is achieved. STRABO. Allegorically. The war of Abram with four kings signifies the war of virtues and vices. The father of faith, therefore, and the first way of believing, fought for his brother Lot and conquered, not in a multitude of army but with three hundred and eighteen ready house-born servants. So let each fight for his soul against spiritual wickedness with three hundred and eighteen home-born servants, that is, with the help of the holy cross: for the letter tau, which has the figure of the cross, expresses three hundred. Dan is one of the sources of the Jordan; the other is called Jor, which is interpreted stream; the two sources, which are not far from each other, joined into one stream, is called the Jordan.
14.18: 14.18 But Melchizedek, etc. JEROME. The Hebrews now say that he is Shem, son of Noah, and by computation of years show that he lived until Isaac: and that all the firstborn from Noah to Aaron were priests. Salem was afterward called Jerusalem; the Apostle, recalling Melchizedek without father and mother, refers it to Christ, and through Him to the Church of the Gentiles, because the glory of the head is referred to the members. Since he blessed Abram circumcised, and in him Levi, and so Aaron, from whom afterward the priesthood. From which he wishes to gather that the priesthood of the Church, which has the foreskin, blessed the circumcised priesthood of the Synagogue. And because it says: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, our ministry of the true order is signified, not through Aaron by immolating irrational victims, but by the bread and wine offered, that is, consecrated as the body and blood of the Lord. STRABO. Melchizedek, who is interpreted king of justice, and is called king of peace, signifies Christ, through whom we are reconciled, and who at the end of the age will judge justly.
14.20: 14.20 He gave him tithes. ISIDORE. The patriarch, therefore, knowing, etc., up to partly not denying the pay lawfully owed to those fighting.
14.24: 14.24 Who came, etc. For faith sometimes uses the testimonies of unbelievers; hence the Apostle to Titus 1: Evil beasts, slow bellies, but for the benefit of the faithful.
15.1: 15.1 After these things were done, etc., Fear not. The multitude of vices having been triumphed over, the hope of every faithful person is strengthened by the Lord that he not waver, but await the reward.
15.2: 15.2 And Abram said. JEROME in the Hebrew Questions. I go without children, etc., up to from him they say Damascus was both named and founded.
15.5: 15.5 Look up to heaven, etc. Above He said: Your seed shall be as the sand of the sea, because among that people there were some carnal and earthly, who are compared to sand, because dry and unfruitful of good works; others like shining stars. RABANUS. A twofold signification of the promised seed is given. When the stars are shown, it is said to him: So shall I make your seed, that is, the Christian nation, of which you are to be father, to shine in faith, namely in the light of the resurrection. But when the sand is shown it is said: So shall your seed be, etc., that is, the nation of the Jews will be numerous, but dry and unfruitful.
15.9: 15.9 Take, He said, for me, etc. ISIDORE, on Genesis, vol. 5. The three-year-old heifer, the Jewish people placed under the yoke of the law, etc., up to when by fire the good will be separated from the evil. A heifer of three years, and a she-goat of three years, etc. Because from Adam to Noah, and from there to Abram, then to David, the people grew up.
15.11: 15.11 And birds came down, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 16, ch. 20. Tropologically. In the very sacrifice of prayer, importunate thoughts thrust themselves in, desiring to seize or violate: but with the hand of holy discretion we must guard what we offer outwardly, lest malignant spirits and perverse thoughts snatch it.
15.12: 15.12 Dread fell, etc. AUGUSTINE in the Hebrew Questions. This question must be treated on account of those who contend that these disturbances do not fall upon the mind of the wise man, etc., up to not to be called a disturbance.
15.13: 15.13 Know foreknowing, etc. ISIDORE. The people of Israel is prophesied to serve in Egypt: not that they served the Egyptians four hundred years, but because this number was completed in that affliction, because it is reckoned from the time at which these things were promised to Abraham. Know foreknowing, etc. AUGUSTINE, City of God, bk. 16, ch. 24. It is not to be taken as though the people of God were in that most harsh servitude for four hundred years, etc., up to the people of God was afflicted in Egypt with hard servitude.
15.16: 15.16 But in the generation, etc. JEROME, Letter to Damasus. Moses elsewhere says, etc., up to and they reach Solomon.
16.1: 16.1 Now Sarai the wife of Abram, etc. RABANUS. Abram is not an adulterer if, his wife living, he is joined to a handmaid, because the law of the Gospel of one wife had not yet been promulgated: and he had heard that his race was to be multiplied, but by what woman he did not know, because he knew Sarah to be barren. In the union there was no lustful pleasure, but the pious love of having offspring: his wife also wished and compelled this, who could not have children; therefore she desired to receive from another one whom she might adopt in place of her own.
16.2: 16.2 Go in to my handmaid, etc. JEROME. Note carefully that the begetting of children in the Hebrew is called building up, etc., up to that, as if borne by an angel, she return into favor and submit herself. RABANUS. These two women are the two Testaments: Hagar, the Old, which in the Synagogue nursed the Jewish people liable to servitude; Sarah, the New, which bore the Christian people into the freedom of faith. The sons of the handmaid were multiplied so as not to be numbered for multitude, who are compared above to sand. This people itself, rival in its ferocity and contrary to all good, and especially when with envy goading it persecutes the Christian people throughout the world, and being scattered far and wide, by wandering and trading is burdensome to all.
16.12: 16.12 He shall be a wild man. Or rustic, according to others. JEROME. In the Hebrew it reads phara, which is interpreted wild ass. It signifies that his seed will dwell in the desert, that is, the Saracens, wandering and of uncertain seats, who, raiding all nations to which the desert is joined at the side, are attacked by all.
16.13: 16.13 And she called. Rightly she called His name thus, because He freely takes counsel for the wretched and consoles the humble. Hence: You consider labor and sorrow, and to You the poor man is left, etc. Surely here I have seen the back parts of Him who sees me. Such is that: You shall see my back parts, for my face shall not appear to you. For man shall not see my face and live (Exodus 33). For that manifestation of the wisdom of God no one can see and live. This is the beauty for which he sighs who loves God with all his heart, all his soul, all his mind: for contemplating which, by loving also his neighbor as himself, he builds up as far as he can. His back parts, that is, His incarnation, which He assumed in the last times, we now contemplate by desiring through faith and love, and in the future shall enjoy in eternal contemplation.
16.14: 16.14 Therefore she called that well, etc. JEROME. To this day the well of Hagar is shown in the desert of Arabia, between Kadesh and Bered, which signifies the Scripture of the old and new law, which our Creator, the life of the living, the hope of the dying, gave to mortals with a look of pious compassion, that, taught and corrected from vices, they may merit to be worthy of the perpetual vision of God.
17.1: 17.1 And I will make a covenant, etc. In the Hebrew berith, which signifies not testament but covenant or pact.
17.5: 17.5 Neither shall your name any more be called Abram. JEROME. The Hebrews say that God added to Abraham and Sarah the letter h from His own name, which among them is the tetragrammaton. He was called Abram, which is exalted father; afterward he was called Abraham, which is father of many, for 'of nations' is not in the name but is understood. Nor is it to be wondered that, although among the Greeks and us the letter a seems added, the letter h is said to be added: for the idiom of the Hebrew tongue is accustomed to write h and read a: as conversely to pronounce h and write a.
17.8: 17.8 And I will give to you and to your seed.
17.10: 17.10 Every male among you shall be circumcised, etc. STRABO. This is commanded Abraham for three reasons. First, that he might please by obedience to the command, by whose transgression Adam had displeased; second, that by this sign he might be distinguished from other nations; third, that, circumcised in that member in which lust is wont to rule, he might know that chastity is to be kept and impurity cut off.
17.11: 17.11 The flesh of your foreskin. RABANUS, STRABO. Circumcision done in one member signifies spiritual circumcision, which is to be shown in the heart and in all the senses. The heart is to be circumcised, lest we think harmful things; the eyes, lest we see vanity; the ears are to be circumcised, that is, stopped, lest they hear blood: and so circumcision is to be practiced in all the senses. ALCUIN, on Genesis, vol. 1. Circumcision was commended to Abraham for this reason, etc., up to whence formerly the transgressors begot unto death. Allegorically. Already then, on account of the future sojourning, lest his seed be mixed with the nations, the covenant of circumcision is given as a sign: because it signifies nature renewed through baptism, after the stripping of the old man through Christ, who rose after baptism. He commanded that the home-born servants and those bought also be circumcised, to teach that the grace of redemption pertains to all. There also the names of the parents are changed, that all things may sound newness. Abram, exalted father; Abraham, father of many nations.
17.14: 17.14 The male whose flesh of the foreskin, etc. ISIDORE. It is asked how circumcised boys, who did not make the covenant of God void, but those who neglected to circumcise them, should perish? But they made the covenant of God void not by deed but by origin in the first man, in whom all sinned. For all are born sinners, not properly but originally. Therefore all perish who are not freed by regeneration.
17.15: 17.15 Sarai your wife, etc. ISIDORE. The promise about the calling of the nations is declared in Isaac, son of promise, that is of grace, not of nature, because of an old father and barren mother: and because this was to come about not through generation, like Ishmael, but through regeneration, circumcision was commanded when the son of Sarah is promised, in the type of the Church, not when Ishmael was, who is a type of the Jews. JEROME, ISIDORE. They err who think that Sarah was first written with one r, and afterward another r was added. And since r among the Greeks signifies a hundred, they suspect many absurdities about this name, though even if they wish the word to have been changed, it ought to have a reason not Greek but Hebrew. For it is Hebrew. No one calling someone in one language takes the etymology of the word from another. Sarai therefore was first called with shin, resh, yod. The yod being taken away, the letter he was added, which is read as a, and she was called Sarah. Before, she was called my princess, because she was as it were mother of one family: afterward simply princess, that is, to be princess of all nations. Some very badly suspect that she was first called leprosy, and afterward princess, since leprosy is called sarai, which in our tongue seems to have some similarity, but in Hebrew is entirely different. For it is written with tsade and ayin and resh and tav; which is plainly distinct from the three above, that is shin, resh and he, with which Sarah is written.
17.17: 17.17 Abraham fell on his face, and laughed in his heart. JEROME. A little later follows: And you shall call his name Isaac: which is interpreted laughter, from the laughter of Abraham, not from the laughter of Sarah. For after his son was called Isaac from the laughter of Abraham, Sarah is read to have laughed. His name Isaac. It must be known that four in the Old Testament were called openly by their names before they were born: Ishmael, Isaac, Samson and Josiah. Read the Scriptures.
17.19: 17.19 I will establish my covenant, etc. The covenant of the Lord is with Isaac, that is, the faithful people, whom mother Church has borne through faith and baptism. And an everlasting covenant, because the possession of eternal life is promised to him alone who with his head Christ will possess the kingdom of heaven forever.
17.20: 17.20 Concerning Ishmael, etc. Historically. Ishmael signifies the people of the Jews, who were greatly multiplied; he begot twelve princes, as the multitude of carnal Jews, begotten of the twelve patriarchs, was divided into twelve tribes.
17.21: 17.21 In the next year. The next year, in which Sarah bore Isaac, is the times of regeneration, in which the blood of Christ was shed and the human race restored to life.
17.22: 17.22 God went up from Abraham, etc. Greek Gloss. Therefore, so to speak, He had come down, and had shown Himself humble, establishing the law of circumcision.
17.23: 17.23 And Abraham took, etc. God did not intend only that the foreskin of the flesh of Abraham and his offspring be circumcised, but He was conferring on him whom He had chosen from all the gifts of the eternal Testament; hence Paul, Philippians 3: For we are the circumcision, who serve God in spirit. And elsewhere, Romans 2: For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, neither is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh. Let us therefore circumcise with the word of God the ears, lips, heart, foreskin and all members of the flesh. Of the circumcision of the ears it is said in Luke 8: He who has ears to hear, let him hear; with uncircumcised ears we cannot hear the words of wisdom and truth. Let us circumcise the lips, that we speak nothing shameful or evil or idle. He circumcises the flesh of the foreskin who uses marriage only for the sake of posterity, at certain and lawful times: he who acts otherwise does not circumcise. The Church, strengthened by the grace of Christ crucified for her, not only restrains herself from unlawful things but even from permitted ones, and as the virgin bride of Christ flourishes with chaste virgins, in whom the true circumcision of the foreskin is kept in the flesh. He who does not commit adultery with obscene desires or heretical senses and blasphemous assertions, but keeps the purity of faith in conscience, is circumcised in heart: and of him can be said: Blessed are the pure in heart (Matthew 5), etc. Let the hands be circumcised, lest they do evil, the feet, lest they run to evil: sight, lest it covet unlawful things; taste, that it may eat and drink to the glory of God; smell, that it may take in the fragrance of Christ, and spread the fragrance of sweetness by works of mercy. Each of the members also, if they serve God in their duties, are circumcised. If they run riot beyond the prescribed law, uncircumcised. JEROME, STRABO. It is usually asked how women were saved, who were not circumcised. By faith, of course, and the offering of sacrifices, as before circumcision holy men were cleansed; whence: Purifying their hearts by faith.
18.1: 18.1 And the Lord appeared to him in the vale of Mamre. ISIDORE on Genesis. Abraham bears a threefold figure: first, of the Savior, who, leaving his kindred, came into the world; second, of the Father, because he offered his only Son; third, that which appears in this place, of the saints who received the coming of Christ with joy. The tent of Abraham signifies Jerusalem, where for a time the prophets and apostles dwelt, and Christ coming was received by believers and hung on a tree by unbelievers.
18.2: 18.2 Three men. Three men announce the coming of Christ, whom two angels accompany, Moses according to some, and Elijah; one lawgiver, who in the law pointed out the coming of the Lord: the other, who is to come at the end, to announce the second coming of Christ and preach His Gospel. Hence when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain they are seen with Him. He saw three and adored one, showing the Savior, whose coming he awaited. Hence: Abraham saw my day and was glad (John 8). For he foresaw the mystery of the future sacrament. Hence he washed their feet, to show that at the end of the world there would be the purification of the washing; for feet signify the last things. Whom when he had seen. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 9, ch. 51. Morally. Abraham meets three angels, because the man and master of the house, that is, spiritual understanding, ought in the knowledge of the Trinity to go beyond the bars of the flesh, and as it were go out of the door of the lowest dwelling. Let the care of the flesh, which Sarah signifies, not appear outside for boasting, but behind the husband's back, that is, under the discretion of the spirit, intent on necessities alone, not knowing how to be shamelessly uncovered, but to be modestly moderated. Ibid., bk. 28, ch. 4. Abraham could not have seen the angels, received them in hospitality and offered them food, unless they had assumed bodies from air: for they would not appear, nor take food, unless they had a solid body from a heavenly element. Nor is it surprising that they are called now angels, now Lord, because they are called angels who minister outwardly, and the Lord is shown who commands them inwardly.
18.4: 18.4 But I will bring. He returns to the duties of hospitality, which can be shown even to angels when they assume a bodily form from the elements: which Abraham understanding, adored the Godhead in its unity, and served the angelic dispensation in visible form.
18.6: 18.6 Three measures. These are said as a type of the Church, which was gathered from the three parts of the world into the unity of faith, and like bread without leaven was baked by the fire of the Holy Spirit. STRABO. A measure (satum) is a kind of measure. The three measures signify the three sons of Noah, from whom every kind of men was scattered. The Church is therefore signified, or the evangelical doctrine to be spread throughout the whole world, and multiplied in the three parts of the world, Asia, Africa and Europe. The three measures, from which Sarah makes hearth-cakes, signify the three sons of Noah, from whom every kind of men was born: who, believing in the divine Trinity, are sprinkled with the water of baptism by Sarah, that is the Church, and gathered into one bread of the body of Christ. These are the three measures of meal which the woman in the Gospel leavened: the loaves are unleavened, because the unity of believers must be without the leaven of malice, and the rancor (another reading: bitterness) of wickedness, and the heat of perverse doctrine. Hearth-cakes. They are baked under ashes, so that through penance for sins, baked by the heat of the Holy Spirit, they may be made food acceptable to God.
18.7: 18.7 A tender calf. The tender and fatted calf is the body of Christ, which was sacrificed for the salvation of the world on the tree of the cross. This is the calf that is killed for the prodigal son.
18.8: 18.8 He set butter and milk with the flesh of the calf, because milk signifies the old law; hence 1 Corinthians 3: I gave you milk to drink, not meat, etc. For he had given them the commandment of the law, like milk pressed from the breasts of the two tablets, that is the testament of faith, because they were not yet able to take the solid food of evangelical doctrine. The richest and fattest butter is the evangelical testimony, which like oil is given to the faithful as a sign. He set the calf with milk and butter, because neither can the body of the Lord be without the milk of the law, nor this without the Gospel. They sat under the tree as a sign of the Lord's passion, whose preachers they are.
18.9: 18.9 Behold she is in the tent, etc. STRABO. Abraham is outside with the angels, Sarah in the tent: because it belongs to the strong and learned to preach openly and instruct by examples: to the weak and unlearned to learn and be subject.
18.10: 18.10 And she shall have a son, etc. God promises the barren Sarah a son, saying: About this time I will come; He signifies not the time but the quality of His coming, since through the promised son a faithful people was to be born. Hence Isaiah 54 and Galatians 4: Rejoice, barren one, who do not bear, etc. Which having heard, etc. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis. Sarah is reproved because she laughed, and not Abraham, although he laughed likewise; because her laughter was of wonder, his of doubt, which He could judge who knows hearts. Sarah denies that she laughed, though she could not hide from God, but perhaps she thought they were men. Abraham understood God, but offered the duties of humanity, which are necessary only for weak flesh; it is wonderful: unless he first thought them men, but in whom he understood God to speak, certain signs of divine majesty appearing: as Scripture often attests that God appeared in men, but afterward they recognized them to have been angels.
18.11: 18.11 Now they were, etc. The age of the 'seniors' is less than that of the 'old'; even if old men are called seniors. Hence, according to the physicians, an older man cannot beget children from an older woman, even if the womanly courses still flow. In this respect Abraham wonders at the power of God in the promise of a son, and we can take it that the Apostle put this miracle there. For the dead body was not altogether incapable of generation if the woman had been of youthful age: but from one of advanced age he could not beget: for from Keturah afterward he begot, because she was young. The physicians say that an old man cannot beget from a woman of more advanced age, even if the womanly courses occur to her, but can from a young one. Again, a woman of advanced age, even if the womanly courses still occur to her, cannot bear from an older man, but can from a young one. It was therefore a miracle, because both were old and of advanced age, and the womanly courses of Sarah had ceased.
18.12: 18.12 Shall I give myself to pleasure? etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 9, ch. 51. The care of the flesh, etc., up to what does our mind bring forth other than joy?
18.15: 18.15 I did not laugh, etc. AMBROSE. Or she denied that she laughed because she did not know; she laughed for this reason, because she prophesied.
18.17: 18.17 Can I hide from Abraham what I am about to do? The Lord well commits His secrets to Abraham, whom He knew to be the faithful executor of His will and secrets; from whom He Himself was to be born in the flesh, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden (2 Corinthians 2). He promises Abraham not only rewards, but the justice of obedience of his sons, and that the promises about them be fulfilled. Again it is promised that Isaac will be a great nation, and that in him all the nations of the earth shall be blessed. By these words two things are promised to him: the nation of the Jews according to the flesh, and all nations through faith.
18.20: 18.20 The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah, etc. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis. If we take these words as not of one doubting but of one angry and threatening, there is no question. For God speaks to men in a human manner, and His anger is without disturbance, because He is unchangeable. We often say in threatening: Let us see whether I do not do it to you, and whether I shall not be able to do it to you; or let me know, that is, let me try whether I cannot. But disturbance does not fall upon God. It is the custom of human speech, to which God adapts Himself, to suit human weakness. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 5, ch. 7. Sin with a voice is guilt in action. Sin with a cry is guilt with liberty.
18.21: 18.21 I will go down and see, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, ch. 33. Let us not believe the evils of men before we prove them. And behold He comes down through angels to learn the evils, and finding them entangled in so great a crime, He as it were passed over patience, and anticipated them with the fire of judgment before the day of judgment: He judges with tranquility, so that greater crimes are slowly believed, and when truly known are punished more quickly. GREGORY, bk. 1 Kings, ch. 178, vol. 1. Where would God go down, to know what had been done? Or what would He not know, who is everywhere? But to give an example of discretion to our ignorance, how we ought not to believe grave evils heard, He says He goes down to learn, of whom it is clear to all that even without going down He knew all things. HILARY, On the Trinity, bk. 9. We have God not knowing, yet He does not fail to know. For although He knows that the sins are very great, again He goes down to see whether they are consummated; and if not yet consummated, to know: we understand that He does not then know because He did not know before; but then knows because the time for acting has come. For God to not know is not a diminution of knowledge, but the fullness of time.
18.24: 18.24 If there be fifty just, etc. ISIDORE. The number fifty, from which it descends to ten, signifies penance. Hence also the fiftieth psalm is penitential. If they were converted, therefore, they would be saved. But when God sees the sinners unwilling to be converted to penance, He at once checks the heat of immoderate lust with the fire of Gehenna. He said Sodom would not perish for ten just men, because if in anyone, through the keeping of the ten commandments, the name of Christ is found, he will not perish. For the figure of the number ten signifies also the cross of Christ.
18.27: 18.27 I will speak to my Lord, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 18, ch. 33. Mystically. The more the saints look into the inner things of the Godhead, the more they see themselves to be nothing. Nowhere is Abraham read to have professed himself ashes and dust, except when he merited to have speech with God. And he says: I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust, etc. For perhaps he would believe himself to be something, if he had not perceived the true being that is above him. Hence David too cries out: Remember, Lord, that I am dust (Psalm 10), etc. Morally. Some it does not lift up by swelling of mind, but by works of mercy; some, while they see themselves abounding in earthly things, do not seek true riches, and do not love the eternal kingdom, because they think temporal things sufficient. The fault is not therefore in the sense, but in the affection. For all things that God made are good. But he who uses good things badly, he brings it about that through the gluttony of greed he dies by the very bread by which he ought to have lived. Poor Lazarus had come to rest, the proud rich man torments tormented (Luke 16): yet Abraham had been rich, who held Lazarus in his bosom. Yet he says: I will speak to my Lord though I am dust and ashes, etc. What did he estimate his riches to be, who thought himself dust and ashes? We plainly see in what place he had set himself, who even when speaking with God estimated himself dust and ashes. With what penalty then are they to be struck who do not advance to the highest things and exalt themselves in the least?
1.9: 1.9 And God said, etc. AUGUSTINE, On Genesis according to the letter, bk. 2, ch. 11, vol. 3. On this day it seems to have been made, etc., up to Hence water is gathered, earth appears; for water is slippery and flowing, earth stable and fixed. Let the waters be gathered together? BEDE, in the Hexameron. The waters that had filled everything between heaven and earth are gathered into one place, so that the light, which in the past two days had lit the waters with clear light, might shine more brightly in the pure air; and the earth that lay hidden might appear; and that which was muddy with waters might become dry and fit for sprouts. If it is asked where the waters were gathered, which had covered all parts of the earth up to heaven, it could have happened that the earth, settling, provided hollow parts in which to receive the flowing waters: it can also be believed that the primary waters were thinner, covering the lands like a mist, but were thickened by the gathering.
1.10: 1.10 And God called the dry land Earth. BEDE, ibid. Earlier, to distinguish it from the waters, He called the whole more solid part of the world earth, saying: In the beginning God created heaven and earth. After the world now begins to be formed, and the face of the earth appears as the waters recede, the portion that could now be dry received the name of earth, to distinguish it from the part still pressed under the waters, because it is trodden by the feet. And the gatherings of the waters He called seas. For so are all gatherings of waters called among the Hebrews, whether salt or sweet. And because, through the continuity of all the waters that are on earth, He said they were gathered into one place, He now calls them in the plural the gatherings of the waters, on account of their many-branched bays. Although it is established that there are many seas, yet He says the waters were gathered into one place, because all are joined to the great sea. If any lakes seem enclosed in themselves, yet through hidden channels they flow back into the sea: well-diggers also prove this, because all the earth is filled with waters through invisible veins, which have their source in the sea.
1.11: 1.11 And He said: Let the earth bring forth, etc. AUGUSTINE, On Genesis according to the letter, bk. 2, ch. 12. The moderation of the Orderer is to be noted: although the creation of herbs and trees is distinct from the species of lands and waters, so that they cannot be counted among the elements, yet because they are bound to the earth, fixed by roots, He willed them to belong to the same day. BEDE, as above. It is clear in these words that the world was perfected and adorned in the spring season, in which green herbs are accustomed to appear, and trees laden with fruit. And it must at once be noted that it was not the first sprouts of herbs or kinds of trees that came forth from seed, but from the earth: because at one command of the Creator the dry land appeared adorned with herbs and clothed with groves, which produced from themselves the fruits and seeds of their own kind. For it was fitting that the form of things come forth first perfect by the command of God: just as man, for whose sake all things were made, was formed in the age of youth. AUGUSTINE, ibid., bk. 3, ch. 18. It is also asked about thorns and thistles and certain unfruitful trees, why or when they were created, since God said: Let the earth bring forth the herb, etc. But by the name of fruit a certain usefulness is signified: and the usefulness, manifest or hidden, is manifold, of all things that the earth nourishes from the root. We can, however, answer simply that after sin the earth brought forth thorns and thistles for man's labor: not that they were previously growing elsewhere and afterward in the fields man would cultivate: but that they grew before and after in the same places, before, however, not for man, but after. Hence 'it shall bring forth for you,' that is, that they begin to grow for you for labor, which before grew only for pasture for other animals. Yielding seed. BEDE, ibid. All things were created perfect, and man was perfect in age, and the trees with leaves and fruit: hence it is said, this fruit-bearing tree.
1.12: 1.12 And the earth brought forth the herb, etc. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 19, ch. 12; bk. 6, ch. 16, vol. 1. What the history attests was truly done in such a way as to signify something else to be done. For the earth is the Church, which refreshes us with the fodder of the word and guards us with the shade of its patronage: by speaking it feeds, by helping it protects; so that it brings forth not only the herb of refreshment but also the tree of protection. And the tree. The tree brought forth seed according to its kind, when our mind, from consideration of itself, gathers what it should do for another, and bears the sprout of right action. Hence a certain wise man says: What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another (Tobit 4). And elsewhere: Whatever you wish men to do to you, do so to them (Matthew 7). Look, as it were, upon your own kind toward one another, and learn from yourselves what you ought to show to others. Seed. STRABO, RABANUS. Sementis is of crops and trees; semen of men and animals. Seminium or sementum is the beginning of anything. On the third day, in which man prepares his mind for sowing the fruits of good works: with the stain and the waves of carnal temptations separated, he has as it were a dry land, the temptations set apart, so that he can say: With the mind I serve the law of God, etc. (Romans 7).
1.13: 1.13 And there was evening and morning. ISIDORE, on Genesis, vol. 5, col. 207. The morning of the third day begins from Abraham, etc., up to The evening is in the sins of the people, by which they passed over the divine commands, up to the malice of Saul. ISIDORE, ibid. On the third day He gathered the lower and salt waters, that is, the unbelievers, shaking themselves with the waves of desires and temptations: and He separated from them the dry land, that is, the faithful thirsting for the fountain of faith. But He restrained the unbelievers, lest by the waves of their iniquity they disturb the dry land, that is, the soul thirsting for God, but that it may be allowed to bring forth the fruits of good works, and to love the neighbor, so that it may have in itself seed according to its likeness; that is, that from its own weakness it may have compassion on another in need, and bring forth a strong fruitful tree, that is, a beneficent one, by rescuing the oppressed and offering him the shade of protection.
1.14: 1.14 And God said: Let there be lights, etc. AUGUSTINE, On Genesis according to the letter, bk. 2, chs. 13, 14. Because two days were assigned to establishing the visible world, namely to the highest and the lowest part of the world: the remaining three were assigned to the visible and movable parts of the world, which are created within the world, etc., up to at the beginning, or the lordship, of the night, which happens when it is full. And let them divide the day. BEDE, in the Hexameron. That is, by this division, that the sun illumine the day, the moon the night. For when the stars were made this was added to the increase of the first light, that the night also might come forth luminous, radiant with the splendor of the moon or stars, which until then had known only darkness. For even if the night seems dark when the air nearest the earth is obscured, yet the higher spaces of the air are always bright with the brilliance of the stars. AUGUSTINE, On Genesis according to the letter, bk. 2, ch. 18. It is usual to ask whether these lights are bodies alone, or have ruling spirits and are vitally inspired by them, as flesh is animated by the souls of animals. But about so obscure a matter nothing is to be rashly believed. And let them be for signs, etc. BEDE, ibid. Because before the stars were made, the order of times was marked by no signs, either noon or any other hour. The lights are therefore for signs, etc.; not that times, whether days or years, began from the creation of these; but because by their risings or passages the order of times, days and years is marked.
1.15: 1.15 To shine, etc. BEDE, ibid. The lights always shine in the firmament, but at opportune times they illumine the earth. For at times a cloudy air stands in the way: the sun also, when risen, with its greater light prevents the moon and stars from illuminating the earth. Hence it is so called, because alone, with the moon and the other stars dimmed, it shines upon the lands by day.
1.16: 1.16 God made two lights. BEDE, ibid. We can take 'great lights' not so much by comparison with others as in themselves; as heaven is called great, and the sea great. For the sun is called great because it fills the circle of the earth with its heat: as the moon with its light, which, in whatever part of heaven they are, illumine the whole earth and are seen by all. A great proof of their magnitude is that to all men the same orb of theirs appears: for if to those placed far away it seemed smaller and to those near greater, it would be a sign of smallness. The greater light, etc. BEDE, ibid. The sun, namely, not only in the form of its body but in the greatness of its light, because it lights the lesser light and the stars. It is greater also in heat, because it warms the world, whereas in the days before its creation the world had had no heat. That the moon is seen equal to the sun and of one size, they say comes from this, that the sun moves much farther from the earth and higher than the moon, and therefore its size cannot be discerned by us. For all things placed farther off seem smaller. And the lesser light, etc. And although it happens that the moon and stars are sometimes seen larger in the day, yet it is established that they bring the comfort of light not to the day but to the night. AUGUSTINE, On Genesis according to the letter, bk. 2, ch. 15, vol. 3. For the moon is seen at the beginning of the night when it is full, otherwise not: and by day it begins to be seen before the full, and in the progress of the night.
18.28: 18.28 If there be five. The five cities burned with fiery rains. For all who have handled the five senses of the body lustfully are to be burned in the future fire. What if found, etc. ALCUIN. This need not be taken of every place. Of Sodom it could be said, because God knew there were not even ten there, and so this was answered to Abraham for the exaggeration of the iniquity of Sodom. Ten. The number ten designates the cross of Christ, because the letter X, by which ten is expressed, is formed in the figure of a cross. He said. For He knew there was not even one there besides Lot; this is said to exaggerate the iniquity, as in Jeremiah: See if you can find a man doing justice (Jeremiah 5); as if: Find even one, and I will spare them.
19.1: 19.1 And the two angels came, etc. It must be noted that three angels, an odd number, appear to Abraham, because God rejoices in the odd number. To Sodom they came in an even number, that is two, which number is the first to depart from unity, and is the prince of otherness, as if figuring effeminate softness. They came in the evening, because for the Sodomites the sun of justice had already set. And when he had seen, etc. While Lot runs to meet them and adores, he seems to understand them as angels; while he invites them to the refreshment of the body, he seems to think them men. So the same is to be understood of these as of those who appeared to Abraham. From this place of Scripture and many others the virtue of hospitality is commended. Hence Paul, Hebrews 13: Do not forget hospitality: for by it some have pleased God, having entertained angels. Greek Gloss. It must be noted that where the benefits of God are set forth, God is present; but where punishments are inflicted, angels are sent; that we may know that to do good is properly delightful and pleasing to God, but that to avenge is disagreeable to God.
19.2: 19.2 Wash. This is customarily done for guests, that the affections, soiled with earthly dust, and by sloth and faintheartedness as by dusty filth, be cleansed. Hence in monasteries a prayer is celebrated for those arriving from a journey.
19.3: 19.3 He compelled them. ALCUIN. The angels enter the house of Lot as though compelled, so that his charity, tested and proved, might be rewarded, and that it might be shown how great a good hospitality is. They entered a hospitable house, and freed the host; fire entered the houses closed to guests and destroyed the sinners.
19.8: 19.8 I have two daughters. AUGUSTINE, Questions on Genesis. Whether a compensation of shameful deeds or of any sins is to be admitted, so that we do evil lest worse things be done, or whether it is to be attributed to the disturbance of Lot, not to counsel, is rightly asked? And this compensation is admitted with very great danger. If it was a disturbance of mind, it is in no way to be imitated.
19.10: 19.10 And they brought Lot in to themselves. GREGORY, Moralia, bk. 6, ch. 16. While the wicked oppose, Lot is brought back and fortified inside the house: because every just man, enduring the plots of the wicked, returns to his mind and remains undaunted. The Sodomites cannot find the door in the house of Lot: because corrupters of minds find no entrance of reproach against the life of the just. Struck with blindness, they go around the house as it were, because in envy they scrutinize his deeds and words. But because a strong and praiseworthy action meets them everywhere in the life of the just man, wandering, they grope the wall.
19.11: 19.11 And they struck with blindness. AUGUSTINE, as above. In Greek, that is, aorasia (if it can be said), which causes one not to see, not all things, but what is not needed. For how would they fail seeking the door, if they had been struck with blindness so as to see nothing? For troubled by their own calamity, they would seek nothing further. With this were struck those who sought Elisha, and those who did not recognize Christ after the resurrection while walking with Him.
19.14: 19.14 Going out, etc. JEROME, in the Hebrew Questions. In what follows the daughters of Lot are read to have been virgins; and he himself said to the Sodomites: Behold I have two daughters who have not known man, etc. But now he is said to have had sons-in-law. Some think that those who had husbands perished in Sodom, and those who were virgins went out with their father. But the Hebrew truth has: Lot went out, and spoke to the betrothed who were to take his daughters: the daughters were therefore virgins, not yet joined in marriage.
19.15: 19.15 And when it was morning, etc. ISIDORE. Mystically. Lot, brother of Abraham, just and hospitable in Sodom, signifies the body of Christ, which groans in all the saints among the wicked, whose deeds it does not consent to, and from whose mixture it will be freed at the end of the age, those being condemned to the punishment of eternal fire.
19.17: 19.17 To the mountain. STRABO. Morally. The mountain signifies the height of virtues, to which the angel exhorts, according to Mark 19: If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, etc. But he who sees that he cannot climb, it is better that he remain in Zoar, that is in the little place, content with the lay and common life, than that he seize the mountain of virtue and return to worldly things. Virginity is a high mountain to which the angel exhorts: if anyone sees that he cannot climb, let him remain in Zoar, that is in lawful marriage, because it is better to use a moderate good than to be hurled down the precipices of lust. Hence 1 Corinthians 7: For fear of fornication let every man have his own wife. I cannot be saved in the mountain: that is, being troubled he did not trust the Lord, whom he recognized in the angels, as being troubled he prostituted his daughters.
19.20: 19.20 There is a city, etc. ISIDORE. Allegorically. Sodom is interpreted blindness, and expresses worldly desires: the height of the mountains, the contemplation of the perfect. But because many flee the allurements of the world, yet, placed in action, cannot attain the summit of contemplation, Lot went out from Sodom but did not reach the mountains. Hence Lot says: This city is near, etc. It is called near, and yet safe for salvation, because the active life is neither wholly separated from worldly cares, nor alien to the joy of eternal salvation. To which I can, etc. Those who are not able to ascend to the contemplative life flee to the active life, in which they are saved. GREGORY, Pastoral Rule 3; Moralia 28. To flee burning Sodom, etc., up to hence to Lot it is said:
19.21: 19.21 Behold also in this I have accepted your prayers, because when prayer is poured out to God, such a life of marriage is not condemned; hence 1 Corinthians 7: Do not defraud one another, etc.
19.24: 19.24 Then the Lord rained upon Sodom, etc. GREGORY. Sulphur, the stench of flesh; fire, the burning of carnal desire; when the Lord decreed to punish the crimes of the flesh, the stain of the crime was made known by the quality of the vengeance. For sulphur stinks, fire burns; those therefore who had burned with the stench of perverse desires of the flesh justly perished by sulphur and fire, that from the just penalty they might learn what they had done by unjust desire. STRABO. It must be noted that the first sinners were destroyed by the water of the flood, who had likewise offended God by the lust of the flesh. But the Sodomites perished by a heavier punishment, namely the deluge of fire and sulphur. For although the former exceeded measure, they sinned as it were naturally; but these against nature: therefore they were condemned by the example of the gravest punishment.
19.25: 19.25 All the inhabitants. ALCUIN. The infants in Sodom were burned with their parents, lest the most impious crime of the Sodomites could be noticed if any trace of their origin remained. And it was provided for them that they should not, living long, follow the examples of their fathers and be punished more heavily. The parents too are guilty both for themselves and for them. For the death of children is the crime of parents. Therefore they will be their accusers. It is also some kind of benefit not to be guilty, if one is not glorious; for it helps not to be poor, one who cannot be a king.
19.26: 19.26 And his wife looking back. ISIDORE. Mystically. The wife figures the kind of those who, called by grace, look back and strive to return to what they had left; of whom it is said in Luke 9: No one putting his hand to the plow and looking back is fit for the kingdom of God. Therefore they are forbidden to look back. In which it is shown that those regenerated by grace are not to return to the old life, if they desire to escape the final fire; the wife looking back was turned into salt, made an example, that is, and a seasoning by which others are salted. Hence Christ says, Luke 17: Remember Lot's wife, so as to season us with salt, that we not be negligent, but prudently take care.
19.29: 19.29 For when He overthrew, etc. Scripture hints that God delivered Lot rather by the merits of Abraham, so that we understand he was called just in a certain way, chiefly because he worshiped the one true God, and by comparison with the Sodomites, among whom living he could not be bent to a similar crime. He remembered Abraham. It is clear that Lot was freed by the merits of Abraham, whom Scripture calls just. And it must be known that he was just not like Abraham, but by comparison with the Sodomites.
19.30: 19.30 And he went up, etc. So the married sometimes ascend from the lowliness of the active life to the height of the contemplative. And Lot went up out of Zoar, etc. JEROME in the Hebrew Questions, vol. 3. It is asked why, when he first preferred Zoar to the mountain of flight, etc., up to he ought not to have doubted.
19.31: 19.31 And the elder said to the younger, etc. This is said in excuse of the daughters, because they thought the human race had failed, and therefore lay with their father. But what follows does not excuse the father, and he did not know that they had lain with him; for the Hebrews mark it above with an obelus, as superfluous, as though it were incredible, because the nature of things does not allow anyone to unite without knowing. STRABO. Lot is inexcusable, first because he did not believe the angel; then because he was drunk, and it was sin as cause of sin. JEROME. So depraved suggestion and delight, like incestuous women, lie in wait for the continent, so that, an occasion being taken, they steep the torpid in the wine of deceit and cast them down from the state of rectitude as if unaware.
19.32: 19.32 Come, let us make him drunk, etc. ALCUIN. The two daughters of Lot had learned that the consummation of the world would be by fire: but, as girls not perfect, they did not know that, the Sodomites being laid waste by fire, much space remained intact; and they suspected that something had been done like what they had heard in the times of Noah, and that they were survivors with their father to restore the human race. And although the crime of intercourse with the father was great, it seemed a graver impiety if, preserving chastity, they destroyed the hope of posterity. So they take counsel, and soften their father's sadness or rigor with wine, and on separate nights each receives conception from an unknowing man, and they do not repeat it.
19.33: 19.33 They gave, etc. ISIDORE. Lot in this place signifies the law, because some born of it and placed under it, by misunderstanding, in a way make themselves drunk; and by not using it lawfully they bring forth works of unbelief. For the law is good, if one use it lawfully.
19.36: 19.36 They conceived therefore, etc. JEROME. Moab is interpreted from the father, and the whole name has an etymology. Ammon, however, for whose name as it were the reason is given, son of my kin, or, as is better in the Hebrew, ben-ammi, that is son of my people, is so derived that part is the sense of the name, part the word itself. For Ammon, from whom the Ammonites, is called my people.
19.37: 19.37 She called his name Moab, etc. THEODORET. This one seems more shameless, who wished to transmit her incest to posterity too. For Moab means from the father: the other more modest, who gave her son the name Ben-ammi, that is son of my people.
20.1: 20.1 Departing thence, etc. Kadesh, fountain of judgment; Shur, narrowness; by which patience is figured.
20.2: 20.2 And he said of Sarah, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is usual to ask how at that age Abraham feared danger on account of Sarah's beauty: but the power of that beauty is to be wondered at, which could still be loved. And he said of Sarah, etc. ISIDORE, on Genesis, vol. 6. He was silent that she was his wife, said sister, lest he be killed and she, a captive, be possessed by foreigners, certain that she would be kept inviolate by God, as with Pharaoh, etc., up to Call no man your father upon earth, for one is your Father who is in heaven. And he said, etc. AUGUSTINE. As to what is said to Abimelech about Sarah, And I spared you that you should not sin against me, it must be noted that God did this, when He warned that she was the wife of Abraham, whom he thought his sister. And it must be noted that sin is committed against God when such things are committed as men think either not to be sins or to be light, as sins in the flesh.
20.7: 20.7 He shall pray for you, etc. CHRYSOSTOM, Homily 45 on Genesis. Know that his prayers will give you life.
20.12: 20.12 Otherwise, etc. JEROME. Because in the Hebrew it reads vegam, that is, also truly she is my sister, daughter of my father, but not daughter of my mother, and it sounds rather that she was Abraham's sister. In excuse we say that such marriages were not yet forbidden by law. Daughter of my father. Another translation, more plainly: from the father, and not from the mother; for she was the daughter of Haran, brother of Abraham, sister of Lot.
1.17: 1.17 That they might shine, etc. These things can be understood of the great lights and the stars; so that what was said, to rule the day, belongs specially to the sun, what was added, and the night, to the moon and stars; but what is added, that they divide the light from the darkness, fits all alike; for wherever they go they carry the light about; hence when they are absent they leave everything dark. If it is asked what the daylight could have been before the creation of the stars, we answer: such as we see when the sun's rising is near but not yet apparent: when, that is, the day shines with the dulled rays of the stars, but the risen sun does not yet gleam. ISIDORE, on Genesis, vol. 5, col. 207. On the fourth day the lights shone in the firmament of heaven, etc., up to because after good works comes the illumination by which the beauty of the higher truth is seen. AUGUSTINE, On Genesis against the Manichees, bk. 1, ch. 24, vol. 3, col. 194. On the fourth day, in which in that firmament of discipline the mind works and distinguishes spiritual understandings, it sees what the unchangeable truth is, which shines in the soul like the sun; and how the soul becomes a partaker of it, and gives order and beauty to the body, like the moon lighting the night. And how all the stars, that is, spiritual understandings, shine in the obscurity of this life as in the night.
1.19: 1.19 And there was evening and morning, etc. BEDE, in the Hexameron, vol. 2, col. 13. In this evening the people of God in Egypt offered the lamb, etc., up to he would give hope and faith. And there was evening, etc. ISIDORE, as above. The morning of the fourth day is the kingdom of David. This age is like youth, which reigns among all the ages, and is the firm firmament of all ages: hence it is compared to the fourth day, on which the stars were made in the firmament of heaven. For the splendor of the sun figures the excellence of the kingdom, the splendor of the moon shows the people obeying the king, like the Synagogue. The stars are its princes, and all things founded in the stability of the kingdom, as in a firmament.
1.20: 1.20 God also said, etc. BEDE, as above. After the face of heaven was adorned on the fourth day with lights, the lower parts of the world, namely water and air, are adorned on the fifth day with their own animals. God also said: Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing, etc. AUGUSTINE, On Genesis according to the letter, bk. 2, from chs. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, vol. 3. In creating the inhabitants of the lower part it was fitting, etc., up to Which is not to be understood except as turned into the nature of waters by the quality of the thicker air. Of the living soul. AUGUSTINE, ibid., ch. 8. That is, which are among living souls, as it is said: the lowly of men, that is, those who are lowly among men. Some think this was said on account of the dullness of their sense, or because fish have no memory; but it is quite certain that they have memory. AUGUSTINE, as above, chs. 3, 4. There is a question about the conversion of the elements. Some say that all things can be converted into all, etc., up to for by touch we perceive waters and winds; hence solid earth is mingled with all the elements, but in these grosser ones it is felt more. Under the firmament, etc. Although an immense space lies between, yet the birds that fly above the earth fly under the starry heaven: as men who are on the earth are said to be under heaven. Another translation: Beside the firmament of heaven, because the spaces of this air which carries up the birds are close to the ether. AUGUSTINE, On Genesis according to the letter, bk. 3, chs. 9, 10, vol. 3, col. 284. It must be noted that some philosophers so distributed animals to each element, etc., up to yet they are permitted to hold only the murky regions of the air, which is for them as a prison until the time of judgment.
1.21: 1.21 And God created the great whales, etc. THEODORET, q. 18 on Genesis. Boys need both frights and also straps and rods: by those we terrify them, by these we instruct them. When God therefore saw that we also were inclined to sloth, He made the beasts, like certain straps and frights, that by them frightening us He might draw us to Himself, and we might implore His help. But as those who are perfect despise frights and straps of this kind, so those who have been brought up in virtue do not dread the attacks of beasts. For before Adam sinned, the beasts attended him, professing obedience. And again, as Noah entered the ark, the lion, the leopard and all the fiercest of the beasts followed him like sheep. And lions were present to Daniel, who though otherwise hungry did not dare approach him, because in him they saw the marks bearing the divine image. Likewise the viper, which had fastened its teeth in the hand of the Apostle, when it found in him nothing tender or soft to sin, at once sprang back and threw itself into the fire, in a way exacting punishment from itself, because it had attacked a body in no way suited to it. We, however, fear the beasts because we neglect virtue. Besides, in other respects the beasts are not useless to us: for from them physicians compose not a few medicines to drive away diseases: let no one then, considering the beasts, complain of the Creator, but seek out their usefulness. And every soul, etc. In contrast to man, who was to be made in the image of God and, if he kept the precepts, would remain in perpetual immutability. The other animals were so made that some serve as food for others or fail with old age.
1.22: 1.22 And He blessed them, etc. AUGUSTINE, Unfinished Book on Genesis, ch. 15, vol. 3. He willed the blessing to avail for fruitfulness, which appears in the succession of offspring, so that by that blessing by which weak and mortal things were created, they might preserve their kind by being born. CHRYSOSTOM, Homily 7 on Genesis, vol. 4, col. 66. The blessing itself, then, is to be increased and multiplied in great number and multitude. For because the animate creatures were animals, and wished to exist perpetually, therefore He added: Increase. For that word preserves them to this present day. Increase and multiply, etc. BEDE, in the Hexameron. It pertains to both kinds of living creatures made from the waters, that is, fish and birds. For as all fish can live only in waters, so too very many birds; which, if they sometimes rest on land and produce young, yet live not from the earth but from the sea, and use the sea more willingly than the land. Mystically. ISIDORE and AUGUSTINE, as above. On the fifth day were made in the waters the creeping things of living souls, that is, men renewed to life by the sacrament of baptism. The flying creatures were made, that is, souls flying to the things above. On the fifth day the advanced mind begins to work in the actions of the turbulent world, as in the waters of the sea, for the benefit of fraternal society, and from corporeal knowledge which pertains to the sea, that is, this life, to produce creeping things of living souls, that is, works that profit living souls; and great whales, that is, the strongest forms of knowledge, by which the waves of the world are broken and despised; and the fowls of heaven, that is, voices proclaiming heavenly things.
1.23: 1.23 And there was evening and morning, etc. AUGUSTINE, On Genesis against the Manichees, bk. 2, ch. 23, vol. 3. Mystically, the morning is the migration into Babylon, when through that captivity the people were placed in a light idleness in a foreign land, etc., up to because they were so blinded that they could not recognize Christ.
1.24: 1.24 And God said: Let the earth bring forth, etc. BEDE, in the Hexameron, vol. 3, col. 13.
